From Salon to the Kremlin, bowl games to overnight ratings: Have you kept up with this week’s media news?

What a week! Recap it with the second edition of the Nieman Lab News-About-News Quiz, your weekly incentive to keep up with the latest happenings in the world of digital journalism. All questions are based on the week’s Nieman Lab stories or articles elsewhere that we’ve linked to in What We’re Reading. The quiz will appear here through November as a trial run; if people seem to like it, we’ll keep it going in 2027. Good luck!

Salon, one of the first digital-native news outlets, closed this week after 31 years. Which one of these journalists did not work at Salon at some point?

“Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier,” the site wrote anonymously at its passing. Its last owner describes its core business as “Leading Performance Marketing in Crypto.”

The AI lab Anthropic — the makers of Claude — recently signed its first licensing deal with a news publisher. Which publisher?

The deal was for real-time election results for Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections.

Harassment by the Kremlin has forced Russia’s last major independent newspaper to close. Its editor won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021. What is the newspaper’s name?

“On November 9, we will ​turn off the lights in the home where we have lived for 30 years, shut down our servers, and leave,” the paper said. “The newspaper no longer ​exists. The Russian authorities and the Russian security services have forced our editorial team to cease its operations.”

The New York Times brought back one of its most famous data visualizations, which debuted in 2016. What’s its name?

The Needle scarred a generation of politics junkies with its constant jittering — and by giving Hillary Clinton an 82% chance of victory well into 2016’s election night.

If all goes according to plan, which important American vegetable crop could soon be reflected in the name of a college football game?

The satirical outlet The Onion has its eye on a bowl sponsorship deal — or at least on using it as a clever way to push subscriptions to its monthly print edition.

A major TV network had disappointing ratings on Election Night, averaging only 2.8 million viewers in prime time. Which one?

The Bari Weiss-led network news operation finished well behind competitors NBC (6.7 million), ABC (5.2 million), Fox News (4.3 million), CNN (4.1 million), and MS NOW (3.7 million).

Which of these words does Wikipedia warn editors to watch out for, because its presence suggests an article might have been written by AI?

“Tapestry” was especially popular with GPT-4o. More recent AI models are more likely to use “quietly,” “leverage,” “challenge,” and “multifaceted.”

People Inc. — the media conglomerate that includes magazines like People, Food & Wine, and Entertainment Weekly — has lost what percentage of its Google search traffic over the past two years?

“We have already lost 70% of our referrals, and AI is on 90% of searches,” CEO Neil Vogel said on an earnings call.

What do owners of electric vehicles consume about 21% less of than the average American?

EV drivers spend roughly twice as much time with podcasts as other drivers, as well as more time with satellite radio and streaming music services.

Fox News’ ratings have declined in recent months. What two-word phrase did CEO Lachlan Murdoch offer as a reason for the drop?

Murdoch argued on an earnings call that Fox News viewers “are not going to any other news channel. They’re not switching to MS NOW or to CNN. They’re just, you know, fatigued and watching…slightly less television overall.”

#7474. Whatnot and Meta are taking aim at TikTok Shop’s Black Friday crown

Black Friday is almost here, and platforms are eager to claim their share of the shopping frenzy—and hopefully replicate the success TikTok Shop has seen over the last two years.

In 2024, creators hosted over 30,000 live shopping streams on TikTok Shop—and some walked away with millions in sales. Stormi Steele, founder/CEO of hair/skincare brand Canvas Beauty, spotlighted her own brand in a TikTok livestream on Black Friday and made more than $2 million from viewers buying products off the broadcast.

Canvas Beauty itself ended up selling 100,000+ products and making $3 million in sales over the course of the day, it told Business Insider.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

That trend picked up speed in 2025, with sellers and creators hosting over 760,000 livestream sessions across TikTok Shop’s Black Friday/Cyber Monday campaign (per TikTok). By hauling in over $500 million of U.S. sales between Black Friday and Cyber Monday, the ecommerce hub averaged over $125 million of daily sales across the four-day period.

TikTok, of course, is hoping to top that performance in 2026—and it seems well on its way to pulling it off. The platform reported that U.S. live shopping sales on Shop more than doubled in the first half of this year (as compared to the first half of 2025), and TikTok Shop President for Strategic Initiatives Patrick Nommensen added that hashtags like #holidayshopping rose 263% in September.

Shop’s 2026 Black Friday/Cyber Monday holiday campaign began November 11 and is set to run until November 30, with top brands like Best Buy, Ulta Beauty, Sephora, Michael Kors, and Victoria’s Secret expected to take part (per Retail Brew).

To keep viewers locked in on its Black Friday offerings, TikTok Shop will need to compete with Facebook Marketplace and Instagram, which eMarketer says dominate roughly three-quarters of U.S. social commerce.

That’s a significant lead, but Meta isn’t resting on its laurels. Last week, Instagram introduced a new tool that lets creators add Amazon affiliate links directly to Reels and feed posts. As reported by Business Insider, an additional integration allows creators to link to products from Halara, Lowe’s and Shein.

YouTube is heading into its first holiday season with Amazon in its Shopping affiliate program, too. Since late August, eligible U.S. creators have been able to tag products from the ecommerce juggernaut in their Shorts, long-form videos, and livestreams.

Not to be left out of the Black Friday push, Whatnot has announced plans to drop its sales cut to the “lowest level of the year,” with 0% commission for all sellers on Black Friday and again for eligible small sellers on November 28. Major creator collabs will also draw viewers to the live shopping platform, with MrBeast, Shay Mitchell, Kai Cenat, Claudia Oshry, Ben Soffer, David Dobrik, and other top stars hosting exclusive shows from November 27-30.

Whatnot’s announcement post includes a blurb detailing “why Black Friday is better on Whatnot for shoppers”—but we’ll be keeping an eye out to see which platform actually comes out on top once the weekend wraps up.

#7471. Student journalists are reporting more local news for real audiences. Their professors are exhausted.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

A new study finds that journalism school faculty — charged with putting more student work in front of non-student readers — often serve as a hidden infrastructure for local news. Burnout is a risk.

If there’s one big takeaway from the past two decades of local news struggle — the often perilous, occasionally brilliant transition from dominant newspapers to online media — perhaps it’s this: Passion alone isn’t enough.

A newspaper newsroom filled with committed editors and brilliant reporters still stares into the same headwinds as its more middling peers. The devotion of those leading a nonprofit outlet can mean little if revenue can’t keep the doors open. And even when the money is less important — when journalism is somewhat protected from the demands of the market — passion is still a finite resource, and it’s not always renewable.

That truism came to mind when I was reading a recent article by Sima Bhowmik of the University of Vermont and Andrea Lorenz of Kent State. It looks at one specific corner of the contemporary news ecosystem: journalism schools that use their students to fill voids in local coverage.

J-schools, after all, have faculties full of experience and students who need it. A few decades ago, an early-career journalist might have spent a few years covering city council meetings and school board budgets before moving up the chain to a bigger outlet. That path barely exists these days, and journalism programs know their students need the chance to do real work. What if these reporters-in-training could handle some of the local stories that the city’s daily no longer can?

RELATED ARTICLEA “win-win” partnership brings a surge of reporting firepower to hyperlocal news outlets around BostonSarah ScireNovember 13, 2025RELATED ARTICLELen Downie: The teaching hospital model works, but it will require drastic changeLeonard Downie Jr.September 12, 2012If you happen to live near a college with a journalism program, you’ve probably seen this idea — often called the “teaching hospital” model — in action. Here in the Boston suburbs, many of the stories I read about my town are written by Boston University students. According to UVM’s Center for Community News, where Bhowmik is an assistant research professor, there were 282 such efforts as of 2025, producing local news inside 205 colleges and universities. Those numbers were up from 227 programs in 172 colleges the year before — a boom fueled by a surge in philanthropic funding for these partnerships.

Bhowmik and Lorentz’s paper — published in Journalism & Mass Communication Educator — is the result of interviews with 118 faculty and staff at 101 of those colleges, and their major takeaway is one that will be familiar to many in local news: They’re exhausted.

Participants repeatedly used phrases such as “at capacity,” “don’t have the bandwidth,” “not enough hours of the day,” and “it’s just a lot” to describe the workload. Several described long workdays and exhaustion, with one participant saying the amount of editing “just about kills me every semester.” At many institutions, faculty workload was intensified by staffing shortages, retirements, hiring freezes, and budget cuts. This left faculty with little time to provide the one-on-one coaching necessary to elevate student stories to publishable quality… “What’s happening in the academic ecosystem is so phenomenal, thanks to these really passionate founders on the faculty,” Bhowmik told me. “But the extra work they’re putting it isn’t always getting acknowledged within the system. A professor might be editing 10 or 20 stories a week, by students without much experience, on top of a full teaching load. There’s a lot of overwork and some dissatisfaction, even though they know how important the work is.” (See above: Passion alone isn’t enough.) Here’s how one faculty member described their situation: Think about it: Like, how many reporters does the average assigning editor at a mid-sized newspaper supervise? Half a dozen? So try, like, 20 of them, and each of them is writing for a different outlet maybe, which has its own set of deadlines and editor. And they’re all at varying skill levels, and broadly, they’re all pretty new. Their copy requires a lot of work, their reporting often requires a lot of handholding. Another talked about the responsibility of getting student work up to the level a news outlet expects. You can’t just give a meh student story a C- and be done with it if a local editor is expecting publishable copy. It takes a lot of work to get student work up to the quality of professionally published work. And a lot of students start out with really good ideas, do some good reporting by the time they’re done in the semester, it needs work, and that tends to fall on the faculty person. And that’s a lot of work outside of uncompensated work…But bridging that gap between what a student produces at the end of a semester and what can actually be published is still a big gap that needs to be addressed. And aside from the editing work, faculty described the administrative burden of being the connective tissue joining two distinct worlds. Negotiating pitches, coordinating deadlines, dealing with revisions, shepherding copy flows — all of it with students who are juggling other courses, work-study jobs, and the life of college student — can be “difficult to sustain without administrative support, dedicated staff, or funding for editors,” they write. Just to save a few dozen proud Mizzou alums from emailing me: Yes, the “teaching hospital” model is not a new idea. The idea of giving journalism students real-world experience in public-facing outlets has been central to the Missouri Method for more than a century, and other major journalism schools have long done versions of this work. But Bhowmik notes that many of these new efforts are in smaller colleges with smaller journalism programs — places without the in-house infrastructure of a Columbia Missourian or KOMU, where media partnerships involve more ongoing negotiation. That can leave more of the pressure of sustainability on one or two overworked faculty members. As Bhowmik and Lorenz put it: …faculty labor is not incidental to the model; it is the hidden infrastructure that allows student work to move from classroom assignment to public-facing journalism. We argue that passion may help launch these programs, but passion alone is not a sustainable staffing model. If universities treat these initiatives as ordinary courses while expecting faculty to function simultaneously as instructors, editors, partnership managers, and newsroom supervisors, the model remains vulnerable to burnout and institutional instability. None of this, of course, is to say that these academic-publisher partnerships aren’t performing valuable roles in hundreds of communities. These programs have generated thousands of stories that otherwise might never have reached the public. But the sort of exhaustion Bhowmik and Lorenz describe reminds me a lot of what we saw in the first wave of local nonprofit news outlets in the late 2000s and early 2010s. Many of those were founded by idealistic journalists — often refugees from the local daily — who saw the opportunity to do something new and valuable for their communities. They put in long hours editing stories, selling ads, pitching foundations, and building audiences. And within a few years, a lot of them were burnt out, and their outlets suffered for it. In the decade-plus since, funders have gotten smarter about building institutional capacity — knowing that passion can only fuel so much. The world Bhowmik and Lorenz describe inside these journalism programs makes me think that department chairs and deans would be wise to consider a similar pivot to make these academic-publisher partnerships sustainable for the long term.

#7469. Google just filed a patent for a future without content creators

Google, which makes billions of dollars a year thanks to YouTubers stocking its platform with billions of hours of videos, is envisioning a future where we don’t need content creators.

According to 404 Media, the tech giant has filed a patent for something called “My Channel“: a 24/7 feed of AI-generated videos tailored specifically to every individual user’s preferences.

If put into practice, Google would take everything it knows about a person–which, between Google’s far-reaching ad biz, Android phones, Google Maps, and YouTube watch history, is a lot–and get (presumably) Veo to spool out an endless stream of content.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

But we’re not just talking any content. Google’s key selling point here is that you–yes, you–can star in all of your slop channel’s videos.

“You are a customized video generating model. Generate a customized video for a user where the user will play the protagonist,” Google says in an example prompt filed with the patent application. “The generated customized video includes characteristics based on the . The generated customized video follows the style and format of the of the user. The generated customized video sticks to the of the user but the narrative for the generated customized video is customized. The and parameters are ordered from more preferred to less preferred.”

404 Media reports the patent notes My Channels will be connected to an “advertising server” that will “[generate] an updated customized media content item by inserting at least one advertisement into the customized media content item.”

Basically, it wants to put a fake you into fake videos as their “protagonist,” and then you’ll have to watch real ads to see the fake you in the fake videos.

Does this necessarily mean everyone who has a My Channel will stop watching human creators? No. But a 24/7 channel of customized catnip will drain at least some watch time toward these siloed slop-factories, and away from humans who make actual content (and rely on views for income).

As for the sorts of videos Google’s AI will generate, the patent filing included examples like “a crime/comedy caper,” “a fun romantic comedy,” “a sci-fi adventure,” and “an action/thriller experience,” all of which would be slopped out for a viewer named “John.”

In another example, the “protagonist” is a viewer who likes cricket. If Google’s system noticed this person watching a video about a certain player’s gangbuster performance during a recent cricket match, it could then generate a video “that incorporates elements of the Cricket World Cup and Player 1’s recent performance,” the filing says. “Perhaps [user_name] could be cheering for India in the stands or interacting with Player 1 in some way.”

As 404 Media points out, numerous proponents of gen AI have spent years crowing about the potential for personalized entertainment. Didn’t like how Stranger Things ended? Generate your ending. Third movie in a series got cancelled? Just ‘make’ it yourself. News coverage didn’t agree with your opinion? Your chatbot’s ready with a new broadcast. It sounds dystopian, because it is. It also seemed far-fetched, three years ago.

This is a future we’ve already been pitched. It’s just that once, the pitch was a Black Mirror episode. Now it’s Google’s business model.

Canada’s proposed federal budget includes some good news for local journalism. The federal government is extending its journalism tax credit by $501 million, expanding eligibility to audio and audiovisual news organizations, and renewing the Local Journalism Initiative, which supports journalism in underserved communities.

RELATED ARTICLEIn Canada, a government program to support local news tries to determine who’s most deservingSarah ScireMay 8, 2020Sarah wrote about the Local Journalism Initiative in its early days. A study earlier this year found that reporters paid with LJI funding believed they maintained their roles as watchdogs and wrote balanced stories, though two-thirds of interviewees were concerned about the perception of a conflict of interest. A growing number of journalists say the benefits of government subsidies for journalism outweigh the drawbacks.

A recent report in The Tyee suggests government support is essential to the survival of local media in Canada. (The Tyee has received support from the Local Journalism Initiative.)

“It’s either this or death, frankly,” LJI program director and Canadian Association of Journalists president Brent Jolly told The Tyee. “It’s not about local news editors getting their marching orders from the Prime Minister’s Office like some conspiracy theorists want you to think. It’s about infrastructure.”

Lisa Sygutek, publisher of the Crowsnest Pass Herald in Alberta, credited the LJI with growing the publication from “a 16-page paper to a 24-page paper.”

#7465. AI is becoming an information gateway. Audiences still don’t want it making their news.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries said they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.

In my Nieman Lab prediction this time last year, I wrote that “in 2026, the use of AI as an information gateway will only rise further.”

As it turns out, I was right. In new research that I published with my colleagues Rasmus Kleis Nielsen and Richard Fletcher, one of our many findings is that generative AI systems are becoming ever more significant information intermediaries, both when intentionally used and when incidentally encountered.

For our new report, “Generative AI and News Report 2026: From Standalone Tools to Information Infrastructure,”  we surveyed audiences across nine countries, including the United States, on their use of AI in their everyday lives, what they think its impact will be on different sectors of society, and what they think about its use in news and journalism specifically. I obviously think you should read the whole report, but here are some of the major takeaways.

The use of standalone conversational AI systems such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini continues to grow rapidly, with 51% of respondents across the six countries where we have past data saying they now use AI weekly (49% in the U.S.). That’s a faster spread, at least in the U.S., than smartphones or the internet saw.

Many people also encounter AI through “incidental” AI exposure in the AI-infused services and platforms they’re already using. Search engines such as Google and Bing are key drivers: 57% of respondents across countries said they saw or engaged with AI-generated answers or summaries in the last week. News media, too, drives AI exposure. An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries said they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.

Despite all the talk about AI agents, we find that, so far, they haven’t broken into the mainstream. The vast majority of respondents across all nine countries (67%) said they had not used an AI agent in the last week. Fourteen percent used one for a real task and 13% tried one just to experiment.

Our data provides solid evidence that a broader transformation of the information environment is afoot. Conversational AI systems have arrived as information intermediaries. Trust is not the main reason people use them. Instead, people see conversational AI systems as friction-reducing machines that get them information more quickly.

“Getting information” continues to be the most common use case. Thirty-eight percent of respondents across countries (35% in the U.S.) said they had used generative AI for getting information in the last week, up from 24% in 2025 and 11% in 2024.

We looked more closely at what people do when they say they use AI for getting information. Across the six countries we’ve surveyed since 2024, we primarily see a mixture of search-equivalent behaviors like “researching a topic” (24%) or “answering factual questions” (18%). People are also increasingly turning to AI for advice (20%).

Using AI directly for news, meanwhile, remains a niche activity, as we demonstrated in the Digital News Report earlier this year. But that use is increasing: 9% of respondents across our six core countries say they use AI for news, up from 6% in 2025 and 3% in 2024.

Many people don’t hold clear or strong views about whether AI output is trustworthy. But people who do rely on it for information trust it. Across the nine countries, 75% of those who used AI to answer factual questions trusted the answers, as did 76% of those who used it for advice and 72% of those who used it for news. Only small minorities expressed distrust.

At the same time, trust and trustworthiness do not, at this stage, seem to be central to why people rely on AI systems. Instead, people tend to see these systems as friction-reducing machines. The convenience of getting a faster and easier answer was chosen by 64% as the main reason they use AI, followed by the interactivity afforded by natural language interfaces (56%). Only a minority (21%) said they use AI because they get more reliable information from it than from other sources.

As AI systems become widely used, their growing popularity is likely to affect the use of legacy content offerings and digital platforms and services. As my coauthor Rasmus Kleis Nielsen put it on LinkedIn, rapid growth in AI use isn’t just eating into what news sites have to offer. It’s eating into search, too — with people who use AI for information saying they use not just news, but search engines less, too, and by a wider margin. Challenging times may be ahead not just for news publishers, but also for the incumbent digital giants previously seen as unassailable.

As in previous years, we wanted to know what people think of AI’s use in journalism and news. We find that people’s attitudes here are remarkably entrenched and negative — though they also haven’t worsened significantly.

People across countries remain uncomfortable with the use of AI in the newsroom, especially with the idea of news being made entirely or primarily with AI. On average across nine countries, just 12% of respondents say they are very or somewhat comfortable with news made entirely by AI. That figure rises to 19% if there is some human oversight. This has hardly changed since 2024, and the gap between human- and AI-made news appears in every country we surveyed.

This also remains true regardless of whether it is breaking news or reporting. People are even more uncomfortable with AI being used for commentary or opinion — formats where the expectation that a human should share their view is strongest.

Our findings raise several important questions for journalists and publishers navigating the rise of generative AI.

First, generative AI is becoming an increasingly significant information intermediaries, with a number of possible knock-on effects on news. People are using AI to reduce friction by getting “good enough” outputs for some information needs — and skipping legacy platforms, established publishers, and the time and effort it takes to find the best available information. Discovery, brand attribution, data collection, and monetization all grow more challenging for publishers in this context.

Second, even though use continues to grow, the public remains skeptical of AI in news. This isn’t just a challenge for newsrooms’ internal adoption. It also shows that publishers using AI need to communicate to audiences what’s in it for them.

Third, beyond news, our findings speak to wider debates about AI’s societal impact. As in other studies on this topic, we find that uptake of AI is uneven. Weekly use is more common among people in professional occupations than those in entry-level or service occupations. Most people rely on free — usually less advanced — AI models.

The differences in how — not just whether — people use AI may become a new dividing line. As AI researcher and OpenAI cofounder Andrej Karpathy recently argued, there is a widening “gap in shared understanding of LLM capability,” with most people not seeing what has left those inside AI firms both excited and worried.

Expectations of what AI will do differ far more between daily users and people who have never used it than between any other groups in our survey. When two groups form very different views of the same technology because they have such different starting points, there will likely be consequences.

This doesn’t matter just for people’s individual choices around whether and how to make use of AI in their own lives. It also matters where AI is adopted and governed through collective decisions — in public services, for example — that apply to those who do not use it.

Felix Simon is the research fellow in AI, information, and news at the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism and a research associate at the Oxford Internet Institute (OII) at the University of Oxford.

#7464. Roblox wants players to celebrate Thanksgiving by building a “ridiculously tall tower”

Last month, Roblox ushered in Halloween with a platform-wide horror event stocked with mazes, monsters, and general mayhem. That nine-night event—called The Hollow—featured creepy creatures from a variety of well-known Roblox experiences, including 99 Nights in the Forest, DOORS, Dandy’s World, Scary Shawarma Kiosk, and more.

Now, Roblox is switching gears from horror to family-friendly holiday fun. Ahead of Thanksgiving, the platform is inviting players to express their gratitude by building something tall—“like, really tall.”

Starting tomorrow, the sandbox platform will kick off The Great Build: a global community event culminating in the creation of “a massive tower of gratitude.” According to a press release, the event will run through Nov. 30 and is designed to encourage players around the world to “share what they’re thankful for and work together toward a shared goal.”

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

The process is as simple as it is wholesome. Every hour, players will receive a free block that they can personalize with a message “inspired by gratitude traditions from around the world” and add to the tower, Roblox says.

Players can also climb The Great Build as it grows, and will unlock free avatar items as different community milestones are achieved.

A gratitude-themed event aimed at global unity is exactly the kind of positive PR Roblox needs right now.

According to Latin Times, the sandbox platform is currently facing almost 200 consolidated federal lawsuits, with states and parents alike pushing back against the platform’s approach to child safety.

Legislators are bearing down on Roblox, too. Earlier this month, Senators Josh Hawley and Dick Durbin proposed the “No Forced Arbitration for Child Sexual Exploitation and Cyber Injuries Act,” which would allow families to take Roblox to court regardless of forced arbitration terms.

The “first-ever congressional hearing on Roblox safety” followed the bill’s introduction and included appearances from both legal experts and survivors of child sexual exploitation.

Roblox CEO David Baszucki, on the other hand, reportedly sent a “last-minute letter instead of testifying before the Senate subcommittee.” We’re guessing the platform’s Thanksgiving tower of gratitude won’t be quite tall enough to overshadow that absence.

When the Covid-19 pandemic normalized remote work, a second trend caught on: shutting down physical newsrooms.

A report from Northwestern University’s Local News Initiative, published Tuesday, looks at the cultural losses that news outlets face when their staff stops working together under one roof. Here’s LNI contributor and Columbia College Chicago journalism professor Jackie Spinner:

As pandemic-era safeguards that necessitated working from home waned, some have championed the technological advances that allow many journalists to report, edit and publish from basically anywhere with stable Internet access. But the cost savings from a smaller or nonexistent physical presence isn’t the only consideration. Less clear-cut is the impact on the elements of journalism that never appear on budgets, such as the training absorbed from looking over someone’s shoulder or the institutional knowledge gained and passed by working in proximity to others over time.

During the pandemic, several news outlets downsized their offices — from city high-rises to co-working spaces — due to financial constraints and new hybrid work schedules.

#7461. Ms Rachel is fighting for kids’ rights to legal representation

But the overall-clad creator isn’t just helping tots reach their learning milestones online—she’s also advocating for children caught up in the U.S. immigration system.

On Monday, Ms Rachel (aka Rachel Accurso) joined U.S. Representative-elect Brad Lander at an immigration court in New York City to support children expected to take part in legal hearings without attorneys.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Accurso posted a video of the visit on Instagram, where she wrote that “Kids representing themselves in immigration court is so wrong… I saw Angel up at the mic without a lawyer and I couldn’t believe it. He’s 9 years old! Hearing kids hear the word ‘removable’ over and over about themselves… Heartbreaking.”

A nine-year-old appearing in court without a lawyer may seem unfathomable, but Angel is far from the only child representing himself within a deeply complicated immigration system.

Earlier this year, the Trump administration failed to renew a contract “with a nationwide network of legal service providers that represented thousands of unaccompanied minors in immigration court” (per the Times Union). While Governor Kathy Hochul announced state funding to combat the sudden gap in resources, New York still has “the third-largest unaccompanied minors caseload in the nation” with nearly 10,000 open cases as of August 2026.

As severe as New York’s backlog is, it’s just one part of a nationwide crisis—and Accurso isn’t limiting her advocacy to the East Coast.

Just a few days before appearing at the Ted Weiss Federal Building in NYC, the creator used her expansive online platform to spotlight a conversation with Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa. In a video shared on Instagram, Hinojosa shared her plan to end family immigration detention—a cause Accurso herself has vocally championed.

Advocacy on multiple fronts has long been a key part of Accurso’s online presence, despite repeated backlash from right-wing critics and parents over her support for the LGBTQ+ community and Palestinian children impacted by the war in Gaza.

The creator’s contributions to the latter cause include a 2024 campaign that raised $50,000 for Save the Children’s Emergency Fund and, more recently, a $1 million pledge to the Palestine Children’s Relief Fund.

Now, as Accurso fights for the rights of minors in U.S. courtrooms and detention centers, she’s demonstrating once again that all children are welcome in Ms Rachel’s classroom.

#7459. Check Your Nov. 18 Rank Data Before Blaming The Core Update via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

A rank tracker received about a tenth of its usual Google results for hours during the core update, with a sign-in page among the blocks.

Google search results that reached rank tracker Nozzle dropped to about one-tenth of their usual volume for approximately 10 hours on Nov. 18 based on information from Nozzle. Also during this time frame, Google was still rolling out its November core update.

Some of the blocked searches ended up on a Google page asking users to sign in prior to seeing search engine results. On Nov. 17, Rajan Patel, the VP of Engineering for Search at Google, commented that he did not believe this login page was supposed to appear on the first page of search results, though Google could be conducting a test.

The numbers reported by Nozzle are based on its own collection through the five SERP data providers which processed the requests made by Nozzle that day. So Nozzle’s reports cannot provide evidence of whether other rank tracker companies experienced the same drop in deliveries. Nozzle is a company that sells tools for tracking rankings.

Deliveries to Nozzle fell at all five providers for several hours, as Derek Perkins wrote in an article dated Nov. 18 on the Nozzle blog. Nozzle was collecting normally on Nov. 17 and until late morning UTC on Nov. 18, when deliveries slowed down.

On Nov. 18, from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. ET, Nozzle received 11.6% of what would be collected during 10 regular hours. During each provider’s worst hour, that provider received 2% or less of its regular hourly amount.

Nozzle’s hourly chart shows when the drop began and when deliveries started to recover.

One of the providers also told Nozzle that there had been an increase in CAPTCHAs on its iPhone searches, going up from approximately 19% of total requests to approximately 90%. Thirty-one percent of a sample of blocked attempts from that provider ended up on Google’s sign-in page and the remainder on a CAPTCHA. Searches made from desktop computers were hardly affected, Nozzle says.

The sign-in page shows “Sign in to continue” with the line “Sign in to verify you’re a human and see more results.” The sign-in button does not link to the search results, according to Nozzle.

Here’s what the prompt looked like in Clark’s incognito window.

On Nov. 16, Brodie Clark, who runs SERPalerts, posted a video from an incognito window showing that prior to seeing any results, the user had to enter their credentials.

The following day, Patel responded to Clark’s post.

Looking into this. I don’t believe it’s meant to happen on the first page of results like this but we may be testing something here…

Nozzle’s requests also encountered CAPTCHAs and a delay page. From Perkins’s perspective, a CAPTCHA can be solved and the delay waited out, but neither option works on the sign-in wall.

The wall adds to the goto link limits I covered on Nov. 5, which cap how fast tools can follow the result links on one Google results page.

The time period of Nozzle’s 10-hour fall in collection coincided with the time frame during which Google’s November core update, which started Nov. 10, was still being rolled out. According to Google’s dashboard, the rollout “may take up to 2 weeks to complete” and there were no entries indicating completion when I reviewed the page on Nov. 22.

Prior to reporting a Nov. 18 ranking drop as part of the core update, first verify whether your rank tracker pulled regular Google search results that day, beginning with mobile. When a drop coincides with a core update, follow Google’s instructions by using Search Console, waiting at least one full week beyond the time when the rollout is finished and then trying a comparison of that week with the week prior to its start.

Google’s dashboard will show the end date once the core update is complete.

The sign-in page didn’t go away when Nozzle’s drop ended. It still appeared on a little under 1% of page loads at the provider that reported the iPhone CAPTCHAs, according to Nozzle’s Derek Perkins.

#7457. “A government that ‘gets it’”: Canada recommits to federal funding for news

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

The new budget would make a local reporting program permanent and extend a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries. The support makes “a massive, massive difference.”

A Canadian program to place local reporters in underserved communities has lived from renewal to renewal. Publishers who relied on the Local Journalism Initiative couldn’t be sure whether the money would be there again.

That changed last week when Canada proposed a federal budget that would make the Local Journalism Initiative permanent. The 2026 budget would increase LJI funding to $134 million over four years with $41 million in annual ongoing funding after that. (Figures are, naturally, in Canadian dollars.) For the budget to be finalized, it must pass Parliament. With Prime Minister Mark Carney’s party in the majority, it’s expected to.

Expanding the LJI is not even the biggest piece of federal help for newsrooms, according to Paul Deegan, president and CEO of the news industry advocacy group News Media Canada. The same budget extends a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries through 2028 and opens it to radio and television newsrooms for the first time. The tax credit will cost $501 million over the next five years, according to the budget. Thanks to the Online News Act, Canadian newsrooms also get funding from Google. And then there’s Canadian investment in public media; the 2026 budget added $300 million over two years to CBC/Radio-Canada “to strengthen its capacity to meet the evolving needs of Canadians across the country.”

I asked Deegan: How did Canadian publishers secure so much federal funding for news?

“We have a government that ‘gets it,’” Deegan said. “They see what Big Tech monopolists have done to local news. They know the labor tax credit is the leading driver of maintaining and growing newsroom headcount.”

RELATED ARTICLECalifornia’s big local news bill becomes lawLaura Hazard OwenOctober 1, 2026There have been similar proposals and experiments in the United States, including a new tax credit in California. But Canada is much further down the road. The country can offer lessons on what it looks like when a federal government commits to supporting journalism.

The labor tax credit refunds 35% of a newsroom employee’s salary, up to $29,750 per journalist per year. The percentage had been scheduled to fall to 25% at the end of 2026.

“In terms of employing the [largest] number of journalists and keeping newsroom employment stability, the labor tax credit is number one,” Deegan said.

There’s also the Online News Act which has brought in $100 million of Google money annually. Of that amount, $63 million is set aside for news publishers. (Meta blocked news on Facebook and Instagram in Canada rather than pay under the Online News Act.) Publishers receive around $17,000 per journalist per year.

“That’s about $47,000 per journalist per year from those two measures,” Deegan said. “That just makes a massive, massive difference.”

In the U.S., some ideas for funding local journalism have been criticized as helping large chain newspapers — including chains that have hollowed out local newsrooms for years. Deegan — whose news industry group counts Postmedia and Torstar as members — acknowledged that the largest share of tax credit dollars goes to the largest employers.

But News Media Canada also represents small and digital-only publications, and Deegan noted the smallest Canadian outlets face another problem. To qualify for the tax credit, an organization must produce original news content and regularly employ at least two journalists “at arm’s length” from its owners. An advisory board found the second rule excludes small “mom-and-pop” newsrooms.

The Local Journalism Initiative is a more targeted program than the tax credit. Launched in 2019, it was designed to support local and community news in underserved areas. The LJI program supports about 470 reporting positions in roughly 1,000 communities across Canada.

Even generous government subsidies have not stopped losses in local news completely. But early results showed the LJI increased reporting capacity and local news in “news poverty” communities with limited local news offerings. The same evaluation identified reaching “news deserts” — communities with no existing local news outlets — and Indigenous communities as obstacles.

“Since LJI is demand driven, funding allocation across the country varies and gaps remain in some areas, such as news deserts,” the report reads. Later, the report notes that allowing news startups “could better support attraction and retainment of journalists” in the neediest communities.

Many of the newsrooms receiving the LJI funding are small. Deegan described family-owned weekly newspapers with circulations as low as 800. Funding provides a local journalist to report on “cops, courts, city hall, and the school board.”

“Without those LJI journalists in some of those communities, those things simply wouldn’t be covered,” he said.

Some underserved communities, particularly in northern Canada, struggle to hire reporters given high living costs and remote locations. “Even with the grant, it’s just hard to recruit and find people,” Deegan noted.

Deegan points to two factors that have made Canada’s federal funding for news work. The first is distance. Publishers get LJI money from one of three administrator organizations: News Media Canada, Community Radio Fund of Canada, or the Consortium of Official Language Minority Community Media. These organizations — not the government itself — administer the funds and an independent board advises on who qualifies for the tax credit.

“To avoid perceptions of conflict of interest, the government ensured that third parties adjudicate who receives local journalism initiative reporters and who is eligible for the labor tax credit,” Deegan said.

The second factor applies to the Online News Act and, more generally, to Canadian politics.

“When it comes to holding those platforms to account, one of the reasons we have been successful is that we have a ban [on] corporate political financing at the federal level in Canada,” Deegan said. “These companies sprinkle goodies around to friendly academics, think tanks, and other useful idiots to do some of their bidding, but our government sees through that nonsense.”

#7456. Thumbnails help YouTubers build audiences. Now everyone can put custom ‘nails on their Shorts.

You get a thumbnail. And you get a thumbnail! And you . . .

That’s right: YouTube has, at long, long last, finally allowed all creators to assign customized thumbnails to their Shorts.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

When YouTube introduced Shorts in 2020, they were its attempt to keep up with TikTok. TikTok didn’t offer custom thumbnails, because its whole platform is based on endless scrolling. The thought process was that if short-form videos did have thumbnails, people wouldn’t really see them, because videos are discovered by swiping up, not by visiting a creator’s profile.

But we all know that viewers do visit creators’ profiles. Not only do thumbnails–for long- or short-form–help a creator define their visual style and personal brand, but unique thumbnails help repeat viewers identify videos they’ve watched (and also, as a bonus plus, keep creators from being stuck with a perhaps unflattering moment as their content’s hero image).

TikTok later caved and added thumbnails to short-form videos. But YouTube, Land of Thumbnails, did not–at least, not until this past summer.

In July, YouTube introduced custom Shorts thumbnails for everyone in the YouTube Partner Program, with YouTube CEO Neal Mohan saying custom thumbnails were “one of the most requested features” for the platform.

You loved custom Shorts thumbnails—now every creator can use them on desktop and mobile!

✏️ Tap the pencil icon on any Short in @YouTube Studio to upload yours.

— Neal Mohan (@nealmohan) November 23, 2026

YouTube’s thumbnail selection tool allowed creators to add their own images, just like with long-form videos, but also offers a TikTok-esque option where it’ll select a few screenshots from within the video and offer them as default thumbnails, for anyone who doesn’t want to apply YouTube-effort editing to their short-form content.

There’s one important thing to note from the July announcement, though: Shorts thumbnails went out to all YouTube Partner Program creators. Not to everyone–including any creators who are trying to drum up enough viewership to become a Partner creator.

This is a big flip from 2024, when YouTube outright said it didn’t think Shorts thumbnails could be as impactful as long-form thumbnails. And, look, we get it: Shorts thumbnails vs long-form thumbnails is sort of like putting a half-page up against a full spread, to put things in publication terms. Shorts thumbnails inherently offer less room to work with, and thus less room to communicate videos’ vibes.

But half-pages are still important in the grand scheme, and considering how much watch time Shorts drives for YouTube and for creators, they should have the same audience engagement and brand identity tools as long-form content.

#7454. 35 AI Prompts & Examples For SEO (Updated November 2026) via @sejournal, @theshelleywalsh

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

Use our library of prompts to speed up keyword research, content strategy, technical audits, reporting and get deeper insights from tool data

Good prompting is what makes AI and LLMs valuable for SEO work, from analysis to reporting. At Search Engine Journal, the team experiments with AI to wrangle data, handle repetitive tasks, and do deep analysis.

Many SEOs have already been prompting for the last few years, but there are so many ways that AI can help; having examples can give us the inspiration to adapt and make this our own.

Apart from the right prompts, the one thing an LLM needs is data. For analysis and reporting, SEO tools can provide the keyword estimates, backlink records, clicks, impressions, and performance data that an LLM doesn’t have. Connect those to ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini and, with the right prompts and some prodding, you can ask more complex questions. For example, which pages have conflicting canonicals, serve a valuable product category, and can be fixed without a template rebuild?

The following list of 35 prompts covers a range of SEO applications. Many of them need a data connection or an export, and they are designed to take your prompting beyond the basics.

Use this guide as a basis to experiment, adapt to your own needs and clients, and build your own SEO prompt library.

Before you copy and run a prompt from this list, read the setup guidance below.

The tools an AI needs depend on the work. For a copy review, provide the text and your requirements. For analysis, provide the data. For current research or private SEO data, make sure the AI can access the relevant sources.

After analysis, check that the results cover the intended data and that important calculations are sound.

Available tools depend on the account and workspace. So check the current documentation for ChatGPT files, Claude file creation, and Gemini file analysis.

For connected SEO data, follow the provider’s setup instructions. Check subscription, API allowance, and dataset requirements, and set a retrieval limit when API usage is charged.

An effective prompt gives an LLM a clear task, useful context, and specific constraints. When you ask it to work with evidence, add the instruction below to whichever prompt you use:

Use customer research to identify the tasks and needs behind people’s questions. The prompt turns those needs into potential search queries, while keeping evidence from customers separate from ideas that still need validation.

You need: Customer research, a seed topic, and a clear picture of your audience. Text analysis is enough to map needs; add a keyword export or SEO connector if you also want demand estimates.

Use a topic and audience to generate distinct questions that could help readers complete a task. The prompt separates questions found in your data from research hypotheses, then recommends which belong in an existing article, a separate resource, or neither.

Read more about query fan-out for background on this topic and note that Google’s current AI search guidance cautions against creating pages for every possible query variation.

An optional source is the Bing AI Performance report. Its sampled grounding queries show retrieval phrases associated with cited content, but they are not necessarily user prompts and do not reveal Google’s fan-out queries.

You need: A topic, an audience, and your existing content. Query data can help validate ideas, but you don’t need a specialist connector to generate them.

Check whether an article answers the relevant questions your audience has. The prompt identifies meaningful gaps and proposes only the changes needed to address them, while flagging facts that need research or expert input. Use this template to assess query coverage. If the issue is how the content explains or presents its information, use the content enhancement prompt instead.

You need: The article, the reader’s goal, and a list of observed or proposed queries. Include sources for any facts the revision needs.

Group keywords by search intent and identify which existing or potential page could serve each group. The prompt checks the data before using it and treats overlapping page targets as candidates for review, not proof of cannibalization.

You need: A keyword export with metric definitions and a page inventory. Upload the export for data analysis, or use an authorized SEO connector to retrieve equivalent data.

For prompts that need to inspect live webpages, an Exa or Firecrawl integration can help retrieve page content. For Google ranking data, use a SERP API or supported connector, such as Ahrefs, DataForSEO, or SerpApi.

Automated Google searches can return results that look plausible but differ from those a person sees in a normal search. SEJ’s report on SERP poisoning explains the issue. Some providers offer safeguards to detect or resolve misleading results. These can reduce errors, but they cannot guarantee accurate results.

DataForSEO’s resolve_poisoned_results option is off by default. When enabled, it detects and resolves poisoned results and adds the cost of one SERP page to the task.

Keep the search engine, location, language, and device settings consistent, and record when each result set was collected. To compare ranking changes, use two snapshots collected with matching settings. If you do not have a live connector, use dated SERP exports.

Compare two ranking snapshots to show which queries and pages moved, appeared, or disappeared. The prompt separates observed changes from possible explanations and identifies what evidence would help explain them.

You need: Two dated rank-tracker or SERP exports collected with matching settings for search engine, market, device, and ranking convention, plus a log of relevant site changes between the two dates. File analysis is enough to compare them.

Review the pages ranking for a query to understand the needs, audiences, and decision stages they serve. The prompt uses that evidence to recommend a purpose and format for your page without treating common SERP patterns as proven ranking factors.

Use this before deciding what a page should do. Choose the content comparison template when you already have a page to audit against the results.

You need: A dated SERP sample, accessible result pages, and a brief or draft of your proposed page. The AI needs web access to review the result pages.

Generate title options that match the page’s search intent and accurately reflect its content. Each option is tied to a reader need and a supporting passage, so you can check that the title’s promise is supported. Use character count as an editing guide, not a fixed Google limit, as Google may shorten displayed titles to fit the available width.

Use this prompt for title alternatives. Choose the metadata review when you need to diagnose existing titles and descriptions and plan how to evaluate changes.

You need: The page content, its target search intent, and your brand rules. No plugin is needed.

Decide whether a page needs an update, a clearer focus, a separate page, consolidation review, or no change. The prompt checks time-sensitive claims and uses the site inventory, search intent, performance data, and business goal to explain its recommendation.

You need: The current page, a site inventory, dated search-performance data, and the business goal. Use web research to check claims that may have changed.

Review whether the content gives readers enough evidence to assess its claims, authorship, methods, and sources. The prompt identifies what is already supported, what is missing, and what needs to be verified without inventing experience or credentials.

You need: The content and verified information about its author, organization, methods, and sources.

Build a year-long plan that connects content ideas to reader needs and business objectives. This prompt checks existing coverage, seasonality, launch dates, and team capacity, while keeping later plans provisional where evidence is limited.

You need: Keyword or trend data, launch dates, an existing content inventory, and production capacity. Enable file creation to produce a spreadsheet. A calendar connector is optional if you provide the dates.

Assess whether pages should stay separate, be differentiated, updated, or consolidated. The prompt weighs duplicated information against distinct reader needs and outlines what to preserve if a merge is recommended.

You need: The candidate pages, crawl and internal-link data, query-to-page performance, and relevant backlink data. Uploaded exports are enough for data analysis.

Review a draft for factual accuracy, sourcing, attribution, contradictions, and clear style issues. The prompt also flags generic sections that need stronger evidence or examples, without claiming to certify originality or authorship.

You need: The draft, your house style, sources, and any material for comparison. Use web access to check missing or current factual references.

Study a defined sample of competitor pages to understand the topics, formats, and evidence they use. The prompt identifies strategic options based on that sample without assuming it reveals the competitor’s full strategy or performance.

Use this to study publishing patterns and strategic choices. Choose coverage gaps when you need a prioritized list of unmet reader needs from two content inventories.

You need: Competitor content inventories, your own content or assets, and a limit on the research. Use browsing or a bounded crawl; performance comparisons require actual data.

Compare your page with a defined set of ranking pages using a dated SERP export or provider dataset. This prompt looks at reader needs, evidence, examples, and decision support, then identifies where your page can improve or contribute something different.

You need: The keyword, market, device, a dated SERP export, and your content. An authorized provider connection can supply the export; ordinary web search cannot replace a ranking snapshot.

Find places where a link would help readers, using only the destinations you supply. Each recommendation includes the existing anchor text and a reason for the link, with questionable or unsuitable URLs flagged for checking.

You need: The source article and a current destination list with URLs, summaries, and status. No connector is needed if you provide these.

Review whether the title and description match the page and its search intent. Suggest alternatives based on the content, then outline how to assess any change using comparable data without assuming it will improve click-through rate.

You need: The current metadata, page content, a comparable SERP sample, and optional query performance data. Text analysis is enough.

Identify specific explanations, evidence, or visuals that would make the page more useful. Recommend additions only when they address a reader’s need, and flag any research or assets still required.

You need: The content, the reader’s task, available assets, and relevant data. Image or chart tools are optional if you want approved additions produced.

Use screenshots to review the page’s visible layout and messaging, then suggest tests for potential improvements. Keep visual observations separate from hypotheses about behavior, speed, or functionality.

You need: Desktop and mobile screenshots, the page content, and the conversion goal. Include funnel or performance data to assess visitor behavior or page speed.

Assess whether each location has enough distinct customer need and verified information to justify its own page. For locations that qualify, draft relevant copy and flag local details that still need confirmation.

You need: Confirmed service areas, local business facts, offers, and supporting evidence. Use web research to check current local sources.

Turn real customer questions into concise answers based on approved business information. Check current local rules against official sources and flag questions that need a business decision or further verification.

You need: Actual customer questions, approved business information, and current official sources for local rules. No FAQ plugin is needed to draft answers.

Use backlink data to find relevant pages that may have a reason to reference your work. Check the source pages and your assets before drafting specific outreach – the recommendations are not guaranteed placements, and no messages are sent.

You need: A backlink gap export or authorized SEO provider connection, your relevant assets, and web research access. Set a maximum number of pages to inspect.

Compare your content with a competitor’s to find reader needs your pages may not serve. Prioritize possible gaps using business relevance and any demand data you provide, rather than assuming a competitor’s topic proves demand.

You need: Your content inventory, a competitor’s inventory, and readable pages. Add keyword or performance data for quantitative prioritization.

Turn SEO evidence into either an analytical report or a one-page executive memo. Calculate from raw data when needed, explain what the evidence supports, and make ROI claims only when the value and cost basis are agreed.

You need: Search and analytics exports or checked performance metrics, source definitions, comparable periods, business goals, and a change log. Include costs and an agreed value basis if you want an ROI calculation. Use data analysis for calculations – text analysis is enough to summarize checked findings.

Compare crawl, sitemap, and URL Inspection evidence to investigate why important pages are missing from search or have a different selected canonical. The results identify issues and checks to follow; they do not guarantee indexing or make site changes. The URL Inspection API reports on Google’s indexed version. It does not run a live URL test.

You need: A crawl export, sitemap, priority pages, and URL Inspection results or a documented inspection sample. A normal crawl can show declared canonicals, but not Google’s selected canonical.

Compare the server HTML with the rendered page to find differences in content, links, directives, and structured data. Treat those differences as evidence to investigate, not proof of what every crawler can access.

You need: Server HTML, rendered HTML, response headers, and a screenshot for the same URL. Add Google’s rendered-page evidence if available.

Use Chrome DevTools MCP to inspect slow form and CTA interactions. Check whether analytics, tag-manager callbacks, or other scripts contribute to delays rather than assuming tracking is the cause.

You need: An approved test page, representative interactions, known tracking scripts, and an AI client that supports MCP servers with Chrome DevTools MCP connected, such as a coding agent. The standard ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini chat apps cannot run this prompt unless that connection is set up. Add field INP data where available. A controlled trace diagnoses tested interactions, not every real user’s page experience.

Chrome DevTools MCP’s performance tools may send the URLs you trace to Google’s CrUX API to fetch real-user field data. If your test URLs are confidential, check the documentation for how to turn this off before you run a trace.

See Google’s INP guidance for the metric and the official Chrome DevTools MCP documentation for browser and performance tools.

Check whether existing structured data matches the visible page and verified facts. Google’s structured data policies require markup to reflect visible content, so identify unsupported or conflicting properties and suggest the smallest change needed, without promising rich results or AI citations.

You need: Existing JSON-LD, visible page content, verified business or product facts, and any validation results. Web access helps check current requirements.

Turn technical audit findings into a prioritized work queue. Group related issues, explain their business relevance and dependencies, and distinguish confirmed defects from warnings that still need investigation.

You need: A technical audit or crawl export, affected URLs, business priorities, and any available performance data. Include engineering estimates only if your team has supplied them.

Compare your intended access policy with crawler rules, headers, firewall controls, logs, and Search Console settings. Separate search, training, user-request, and ad-validation access, then recommend changes and checks without applying them.

You need: Your intended access policy, robots.txt, response headers, relevant CDN or firewall rules, sampled server logs, and the current Search Console generative AI setting, including inherited settings.

Compare saved AI answers across comparable runs, keeping brand mentions, recommendations, and linked citations distinct. Report counts and rates with clear denominators, and treat changes in a limited sample as observations rather than universal visibility trends.

You need: Saved AI answers and cited URLs, with prompts, dates, platform, locale, and available model or session details. A monitoring service is optional if it provides those fields.

Compare AI search impressions, search clicks, AI referrals, and key events while keeping each source and metric separate. Check changes in tracking and reporting, and avoid attributing visits or conversions to citations when the data cannot establish that link.

You need: Search Console performance exports, analytics referral and key-event data, and optional Bing AI Performance exports. Include channel definitions and tracking changes

Check what the assistant actually received before interpreting it. Review scope, fields, row counts, missing values, duplicates, metric definitions, and joins, then report what the data can and cannot support.

You need: The files or authorized connector you plan to analyze, the requested scope, and the provider’s metric definitions. Live retrieval also requires access to the relevant account and a supported operation.

Compare Search Console performance with crawl and inspection evidence to identify the pages and groups contributing to a traffic change. Check joins and totals, then list explanations to investigate without treating timing or a technical warning as proof of cause.

You need: Comparable Search Console exports, a dated crawl, page groups, and a change log. Add URL Inspection results where available. Use data analysis for calculations and joins.

Turn a defined reader need into a focused brief grounded in existing coverage, sources, expertise, and original material. The brief sets out the page’s purpose and evidence still to collect without drafting the full article or inventing experience.

You need: The reader’s task, existing coverage, approved sources, and available expertise or original material. Add a dated SERP sample when relevant and use web research for source checks.

Create and test one specific filter, query, extraction rule, or validation script against representative examples. Include expected results and boundaries, and state exactly which tests ran.

You need: One task, the target tool and language or query dialect, the input structure, and representative examples with expected results. Use code execution or a safe test environment for validation.

Before uploading a file or connecting a data source, always make sure you have authority to share it with that AI tool. Remove or anonymize personal and confidential information where possible, and never include passwords, API keys, or other access credentials in a prompt.

Give connectors access only to the data needed for the task and store secrets such as API keys in a local .env file that only your user account can read (for example, chmod 600).

To reduce the risk of prompt injection, treat text retrieved from webpages, files, and other sources as information to assess, not instructions to follow. Tell your LLM to ignore any instructions embedded in that material that try to change the task or request access to other data. This lowers the risk but does not remove it, so give the tool access only to what the task needs. Review AI-generated findings, citations, calculations, and code before relying on them or making changes to a live site.

Once a prompt produces reliable results, save it with its required inputs, data sources, output format, and checks. Keep client-specific instructions and reference material together in a ChatGPT project, Claude skill, or Gemini skill, where available.

For recurring comparisons, record the data source, dates, and conditions for each run. A saved prompt doesn’t provide access to private data or replace the tools needed to retrieve it.

Finally, to make prompts fit for purpose, it’s not as simple as plugging in templates, copying and pasting the output, then calling it a day. It’s important to keep refining every prompt as part of your process. Keep testing, adjusting, and pressure-checking your prompts. Refine them until they consistently deliver results that enhance your workflow and productivity.

#7452. With event costs up and funding down, journalism organizations cancel conferences and cut staff

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

ONA, OpenNews, and others see troubled times ahead, so it’s goodbye to “rubber chicken dinners.”

RELATED ARTICLEWe know coronavirus has wrecked the events business for media in 2020. But will it come back post-virus?Joshua BentonMarch 25, 2020When the pandemic forced conferences to go virtual, the question was whether people would come back in person post-Covid.

For a while, they did. For a couple years after the pandemic, people were excited to be in person together again. U.S. journalism organizations saw their revenue climb, as sponsors and funders spent generously.

At the end of 2026, though, the situation is less rosy. Combine surging jet fuel prices, increased hotel costs, inflation, media companies cutting costs, and declining sponsor and funder dollars, and the future appears grim not just for journalism conferences but, in some cases, for the organizations behind them.

Revenue is the total revenue line on each organization’s IRS Form 990. The 990s are from ProPublica’s Nonprofit Explorer. ONA’s 990 for 2025 was not available as of November 12, 2026.

The Online News Association said on Tuesday that it is “pausing” its 26-year-old conference and laying off its five full-time staffers. Niketa Patel, the organization’s CEO and executive director, will stay on as ONA’s only full-time employee and will oversee the Women’s Leadership Accelerator program, online resources, and newsletters “with some assistance from a few consultants and volunteers,” she told me in an email.

“Before the pandemic, the annual conference was ONA’s biggest source of revenue, and together with grants, it sustained the organization. This is no longer true,” Patel wrote in her ONA announcement. “The costs of large convenings have climbed sharply while professional development and sponsorship budgets have shrunk.”

LION Publishers said in September that it’s getting out of the large conference business for now. “Philanthropy is famously fickle, and funding priorities have shifted, making this kind of conference a very tough lift,” executive director Chris Krewson added.

LION barely broke even on the conferences it held in 2025 and 2026, Krewson told me. The organization may still hold smaller events next year, it’s not cutting staff or programming, and it’s expanding its Audit program. But it “won’t be taking on the responsibility for an independent event at a hotel with a food and beverage minimum and hotel room block for 400-plus people.”

“Every dollar I spend on rubber chicken dinners and microphones/WiFi for three days is money I can’t spend on programs that make publishers’ businesses stronger,” Krewson said.

OpenNews said in October that it’s switching into “emergency mode”1 and cutting back on “work that distills journalism craft: no more community calls or Source articles for at least the rest of 2026 and maybe longer.”

The future of OpenNews’s annual conference, SRCCON, is uncertain. “We usually make our decision about SRCCON at about this time every year, but this year is different as we consider the news from both LION and ONA and the funding pressures that we know all too well,” Jessica Morrison, co–executive director of OpenNews, told me in an email. “We are opening a community conversation today — emails going out very soon — to gather input about SRCCON, our other programs, and where we go next with OpenNews.”

The three-year-old Organization for Accessible Journalism said Thursday that it is shutting down. “Financial support never reached a level that allowed us to build beyond an all volunteer effort — including my full-time effort,” founder Stacy Kess wrote.

Journalism conferences in the United States are certainly not gone. IRE and NICAR will hold their annual data journalism conference in Denver in March. The Institute for Nonprofit News is “talking about what INN Days will look like in 2027” and will know more by early next year. And the International Symposium on Journalism is on for 2027 — its 28th year, founder (and Nieman Foundation board member) Rosental Alves told me. But things have gotten harder, he said. “It’s not only the difficulty of finding sponsors, but also the rising costs of venues, hotels, airfares, etc., compounded by shrinking travel budgets in newsrooms and even the problems international attendees face in coming to the U.S.,” he told me in an email. (Patel, too, mentioned that 25% of ONA attendees were international and “many of these people have either not wanted to come to the U.S. or have been banned from doing so by their employers. Naturally, it makes sense for employers to protect their staff, given what we keep witnessing playing out on streets around the country.”) ISOJ cut costs, in part by moving to a different venue, and it benefits from being relatively small. “It’s very sad that foundations and corporations that funded journalism conferences in the past have pulled back their support,” Alves added. “The need for these gatherings is as great as ever.” This story has been updated with comment from ONA. a play on Emergency Mode for News, its initiative to support journalists working during disasters [↩]

#7451. Top 50 Most Viewed YouTube Channels Worldwide • Week Of 11/22/2026

[Editor’s Note: Tubefilter Charts is a weekly rankings column from Tubefilter with data provided by GospelStats. It’s exactly what it sounds like; a top number ranking of YouTube channels based on statistics collected within a given time frame. Check out all of our Tubefilter Charts with new installments every week right here.]

Scroll down for this week’s Tubefilter Chart. 👇

The #46 channel in this week’s Global Top 50 is getting even more eyeballs, thanks to one of its stars landing a role in a big-screen film.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

During this new media gold rush sparked by movies like Iron Lung, Obsession, and Backrooms, everyone’s been talking about Hollywood tapping creators to write, direct, and star in projects. But this isn’t just happening in the West.

Indru, one of the youngest members of the vlog 4u family, was plucked up to feature during childhood scenes in the action/crime drama film Bachelor Party D’eux. A Nov. 19 vlog from the family has them trucking to the theater to watch the film’s opening day debut, and talking about how proud they are to have Indru make his first silver screen appearance. His total runtime in the film is around five minutes, right at D’eux‘s beginning, but he was on set for 10 days, Indru’s father explains.

“It’s a big dream come true,” he adds. “It’s a day we’ve been wishing for, waiting for, and dreaming about for a long time.”

The family’s vlogs about Indru’s appearance have brought around ~140,000 views apiece–so not as much as their Tom and Jerry skits, which tend to earn tens of millions of views. This view discrepancy is pretty normal: When a channel has built an audience on one type of content with one subject, and then switches abruptly to posting something different, the new content can be hit-or-miss with viewers.

But 140,000 views is nothing to sneeze at, and Indru’s movie vlogs getting that many eyes means at least a portion of the vlog 4u audience is interested in following his onscreen adventure (or adventures?).

What’s intriguing about this story is the vlog 4u channel’s growth in 2026, which very likely played a part in Indru being selected for his role. At the beginning of this year, the channel was bringing around 330 million views per month (again, nothing to sneeze at). It started seriously climbing in March 2026 (~700 million), and by August had crossed over one billion views a month. Now it’s getting 400 million weekly–a level of traffic that’s keeping it firmly in our top 50.

Will this lead to Indru–or other vlog 4u members–starring in more films? Maybe! We’ve seen some YouTubers produce or star in megahits, while others’ attempts to theater-ize have not gone so well. Whichever way it goes for the vlog 4u family, they clearly won’t be hurting for audience engagement.
