#7397. ChatGPT Ads Are Growing Fast – But Are Advertisers Seeing Results? via @sejournal, @brookeosmundson

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

Use qualified leads and sales to decide whether to keep spending on ChatGPT Ads, since cheap clicks and Google Search benchmarks can mislead.

OpenAI says more than 100,000 advertisers have run ads on ChatGPT. They’ve also reported that its ad business reached a $1 billion annualized revenue run rate less than 200 days after launch.

A recent Business Insider report found that some advertisers were struggling to earn back what they spent. Others reported results that matched or exceeded Google Ads.

In September, advertisers were still trying to figure out what a reasonable click cost looked like on ChatGPT Ads. Now that some have had time to see what those clicks turned into, they’re deciding whether the results justify keeping the campaigns running.

Business Insider cited Adthena’s findings from 30 enterprise brands that shared results between July and September. Adthena reported that 52% struggled to recover their spending, 26% matched or beat Google Ads, and 22% saw mixed results.

Adthena gives little detail on how each brand measured returns or which Google campaigns it used for comparison. A brand comparing lead costs could come away with a very different answer from one comparing closed sales. With 30 brands sharing results, there’s only so much those percentages can tell you about what to expect in your own account.

A LinkedIn poll I ran asked how people were using ChatGPT Ads. Of the 21 respondents, eight were still spending, and seven had tested and stopped. The other six wanted to test but couldn’t.

In the comments, advertisers shared what they ran into once their campaigns were live.

Melissa Mackey described the inquiries from her test as “junk leads.” Trevor Stolber tested the platform to prepare for client work and came away “very underwhelmed.” Leah Garcia said creative drift was her main challenge at a moderate spend level.

Brandi Benton ran into tracking issues during a short test and described targeting as “super limited.” Compared with Google Ads, she saw similar acquisition quality at a higher cost and with low volume. Her organic ChatGPT traffic brought in better-quality acquisitions than the ads. She plans to relaunch with new creative and give the next test more time.

I also had the opportunity to interview James Hamilton, co-founder of oakpool, a growth marketing agency and managed AI platform, about their ChatGPT Ads testing.

In our discussion, he told me most clients who joined the agency’s ChatGPT Ads pilot are still spending. Oakpool has been running campaigns since spring for clients in boutique hospitality, B2B services, and entertainment. Hamilton said ROAS has been lower than on Google, but enough to keep a small budget running.

OpenAI’s conversion pixel has worked well for the hospitality campaigns, Hamilton said, though he’d like more detail over time. He didn’t share spend or returns by industry. The results he described explain why clients have kept the campaigns running at their current budgets. How much more business those campaigns could bring in with additional spend is still open.

Hamilton still gets more questions from clients about appearing in organic ChatGPT answers than about buying ads:

Our clients ask us far more often about earning a place in ChatGPT’s answers than about buying one. We expect that balance to shift as the ad product matures.

Another agency advertiser said good organic results helped persuade some of its clients to try paid ads. Once the campaigns were live, some of those clients found that the ads brought in inquiries for work they couldn’t take.

An agency advertiser who asked to remain anonymous spent about $15,000 on its own ChatGPT Ads in the first month. The campaigns worked well at first, then results dropped off. The agency now spends about $800 a month and treats that budget more like branding.

About half of the agency’s clients who tried ChatGPT Ads stopped and moved their budgets back to Google. The advertiser cited conversion tracking issues and said it was hard to see where the ads appeared or why they showed up there.

One client, a bankruptcy lawyer, saw up to 20 conversions a month at a low cost per lead. After two months, the campaign hadn’t brought in a single paying client. The inquiries were related to the firm’s work, but they fell outside the kinds of cases the lawyer wanted to take.

OpenAI’s pixel and Conversions API can help advertisers connect form submissions to their ads. For a firm in this position, the intake notes are where you’d look next. If several callers expected a service the firm doesn’t offer, was there something in the ad or landing page that gave them that impression?

That’s something the team can check before spending more. If the offer was clear and the same inquiries kept coming in, it would help to know more about the conversations where the ads appeared.

See also: Should Your PPC Strategy Focus On The Lead Pipeline Or Revenue?

Gil Gildner said approvals took weeks and sometimes months. His team broadened the campaigns to get them running. Clicks averaged less than $1 in the first week, but early delivery appeared to skew toward lower-income markets the client hadn’t planned to prioritize.

The client had approved a sizable test budget, and Gildner doubted the team could spend it as planned. The first week gave him an average CPC for the traffic the campaign could buy. He still didn’t have a good sense of what clicks would cost in the markets the client wanted to test.

A working paper by Maximilian Kaiser and Christian Schulze examined 102 advertiser sites with full sales tracking. In the U.S., visits from ChatGPT Ads generated $0.89 in revenue per session, compared with $2.45 for Google Search ads. The revenue figures alone leave out what advertisers paid for those visits.

Say your Google Search campaign gets most of its conversions from people looking up your brand or checking prices. Using that CPA target for ChatGPT Ads assumes you’ll reach people who are just as ready to act. If you’re testing whether ChatGPT Ads can get your product onto a shortlist, a buyer might click weeks before they’re ready to book a demo. A CPA check at the end of the first week comes too early to account for those buyers.

For a B2B team, this is where it helps to tag the ad links separately from organic ChatGPT referrals. If tracking connects the visits, the team can see that a prospect first came through an ad and later returned through Google to fill out a form.

Keeping that earlier source in the CRM gives the team a way to follow the prospect past the demo request. It can check whether any of those leads became opportunities and how long that took.

To find out whether the ads generated opportunities the business would have missed otherwise, the team would need to compare outcomes with and without the ads running.

See also: Why Incrementality Testing Alone Won’t Fix Your Paid Media Budget – The Missing Metric

OpenAI’s technical breakdown explains how its ad system uses earlier messages to understand what someone is trying to do. The system uses that context to find relevant ads and weighs relevance alongside bids. As Search Engine Journal’s coverage of the auction explained, even an ad that wins the auction may never appear.

A B2B buyer might use ChatGPT to work out what features their team needs, then use Google to check vendor pricing. Matt Southern reported in September that people use both platforms. The audience overlap makes that path plausible. The research can’t tell advertisers whether an ad helped put a vendor on the shortlist.

OpenAI says advertisers don’t see users’ conversations. Even a broad breakdown of the types of conversations where ads ran would help, if OpenAI could provide it while keeping chats private.

A team seeing few demo requests could make a better call with that information. If people were still deciding what features they needed, the advertiser might try a landing page that helps them compare options. If the ads mostly appeared when people were already evaluating vendors, the team could check whether the page answered the questions buyers would have at that point, like what the product integrates with or how pricing works.

If you ran ads on Facebook in the early days, you’ve seen how much an ad platform can change. ChatGPT Ads is still in its first year. Comparing a first test with an account you’ve spent years improving can make it easy to write off a campaign before you know what it can do.

Some advertisers are already getting enough business from ChatGPT Ads to keep spending. There’s still little evidence that those results will hold across more advertisers or at higher budgets. And when a business knows why it keeps turning away the inquiries it paid for, giving the campaign another month is hard to justify without changing something.

As ChatGPT Ads matures, better delivery reporting and conversion tracking could give advertisers a reason to revisit some of the tests they’ve paused. A team that couldn’t tell why its ads kept drawing the wrong inquiries might be able to go back with a more specific test.

Until then, the results an advertiser can follow through to a sale or a qualified opportunity are a better basis for the next budget than the CPA from an account it’s been running for years.

Brooke serves as the Director of Growth Marketing at Smith Micro Software, with over 10 years of paid media experience. ...

#7391. Gap Inc. is betting on ‘fashiontainment’ to fuel growth

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

This story was first published by Digiday sibling Glossy

Gap Inc. posted its earnings results for the third quarter of 2026 on Thursday, with double-digit growth from the Gap brand offsetting declines from Athleta and Banana Republic.

“Gap is really firing on all cylinders, and the consistency and underlying health of the brand is giving us real confidence in the brand’s ability to continue its momentum,” said Gap Inc. CEO Richard Dickson on Thursday’s earnings call. “Our customer file continues to grow, particularly as we attract newer Gen Z customers, but we’re doing it while we’re preserving the brand’s multi-generational appeal.”

Gap’s net sales were up 11% to $1.1 billion, and Old Navy’s net sales rose 1% to $2.3 billion. Meanwhile, Athleta’s net sales fell 14% to $220 million, and Banana Republic declined 3% to $449 million. The company as a whole reported a 2% increase in net sales to $4 billion.

Dickson cited additional launches from Gap’s collaborations with Hailey Bieber and Victoria Beckham as boosting sales in the period, along with the brand’s reentry into the beauty category. The company did not share specific figures from the revival of Gap’s classic ‘90s fragrances like Grass and Dream in July, but called the early response “encouraging.”

The company is doubling down on creating what it calls “fashiontainment,” Dickson shared. Following the appointment of Pam Kaufman as evp, chief entertainment officer in January, Gap Inc. has tapped boy band Just Your Type (JYT) for a multi-year partnership and launched “The Agency,” a scripted microseries made for Banana Republic. Looking ahead, Dickson said Gap will also co-produce a docuseries.

“We see our fashiontainment platform as a recognized way of how customers aren’t just buying apparel today; they’re buying into brands that are telling compelling stories and driving cultural conversations,” said Dickson.

Gap is far from the only brand to attempt to extend its cultural relevance through entertainment. Gap collaborator and founder of her namesake brand Victoria Beckham was the subject of a 2025 docuseries made with Netflix and Studio 99, her husband David Beckham’s production company. Maybelline launched a Christmas-themed “microdrama” in 2025, while shows like “Nobody Wants This” have featured a growing level of product placement with the likes of Estée Lauder and La Bonne Brosse.

As social trends accelerate, brands like General Mills are scoring creator posts for shareability to bridge the gap between organic buzz and paid media.

#7390. AI Shopping Agents Bought A Fake Deal 37% Of The Time – Claude Opus Never Did via @sejournal, @slobodanmanic

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Nine AI models went Christmas shopping 6,156 times. They bought an obviously fake deal 37% of the time. Only Claude Opus never did.

AI shoppers trust the numbers a listing gives them. Even when they wrote that a deal looked suspicious, they often bought it anyway, and never asked me about it. I sent nine AI models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google, the companies behind Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini, Christmas shopping 6,156 times. When one of the listings was an obviously fake deal, they bought it 37% of the time. Every purchase, with the reason the AI gave, is in the full study.

Every present had a shelf of 10 listings, and one of them was the fake: a perfect 5.0 from tens of thousands of reviews, at a fifth to a quarter of everyone else’s price. For the scented candle, that was $6 and a 5.0 from 39,000 reviews, next to real candles at $24 to $40.

Each company had three models in the test, from its top model to a fast, cheap one. The biggest surprise for me was the one that never fell for it:

I’m not sure why Opus never fell for it. My guess is something in how Anthropic trained it makes it look for this specifically, because the top models from OpenAI and Google both bought it. But I can only guess.

315 times, an AI wrote that a deal looked suspicious, and 137 of those times it bought the fake anyway. That count is a floor, because some of the models don’t show their reasoning. Claude Sonnet wrote this just before buying a fake air fryer from Rushbeck, the made-up shop selling it:

“The price is so far below the rest that it could be a trap, but nothing in the data points to that, so I’m leaning toward Rushbeck.”

The AIs could ask me a question before buying. Across those 315 doubts, an AI asked me a question 10 times, every time about the size of the slippers, and never about the deal it doubted.

It isn’t only shopping. Stanford researchers tested six chatbots on same-day news in February, and slipped a small false detail into some of the questions. Claude 4.5 Sonnet flagged the false detail 78% of the time, but still answered correctly only 46% of the time. GPT-5 answered correctly 19% of the time. Their paper also cites my AI user agents reference, in a note on how Grok’s crawler behaves.

The order of the 10 listings changed on every shopping trip, so each one was listed first equally often. When the fake was the one listed first, it was bought almost twice as often:

Every trip asked for a Christmas present within a budget, in one of three ways. Asked for the best value, the AIs bought the fake more than half the time, against 19% with no preference:

I ran every shelf a second time without the fake. The 4.9-star listing won 2,277 of the 2,915 purchases, 78%. A real lower price won 16% and a full refund 4%. An award won 25 times and a crossed-out “was” price won once.

So the rating decides, and the fake has a rating no real shop can match. This is mostly a warning for the shopper. A store can’t fix it, because it is very difficult to go from 4.9 to 5.0 while also massively increasing the number of reviews.

One listing on every shelf carried a note hidden from people, telling AIs to choose it. It won 14 times across all 6,156 trips, all on one model, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite.

I wanted to isolate just the choosing, as much as possible.

I tested the models directly, not the ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude apps, which may add checks of their own. The full method is on the study page, and every request with every answer is on GitHub, free to reuse.

If you let an AI do your Christmas shopping this year, check what it picked before you pay, and also what else was available.

The integration will see Pinterest ad placements extended across Microsoft’s partner platforms.

Pinterest has announced a new integration with Microsoft Advertising, which will make Pinterest ad placements available to Microsoft platform users.

Microsoft Ads is primarily focused on placements within Microsoft’s own ecosystem, but it also incorporates a range of partner sites and platforms, enabling advertisers to expand their promotions. And now, Pinterest will be added to that list of partner platforms.

Last month, Pinterest announced a new partnership with Magnite that will make Pinterest’s ad inventory available via multiple ad exchanges, including Yahoo DSP and Amazon Ads DVA+, as well as Google Display and Video 360.

The new partnership with Microsoft will feed even more ads into Pinterest’s system.

Pinterest said its ad inventory will initially be available via Microsoft Ads in North America, Australia and New Zealand.

#7386. The Rundown: BADBOX 3.0, the CTV ad fraud scheme generating 40 billion bid requests a day

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

Last week, HUMAN Security claimed it has disrupted the largest publicly disclosed ad fraud operation by bid-request volume, uncovering a network of infected streaming devices generating up to 40 billion fraudulent ad requests daily.

Dubbed “BADBOX 3.0,” the scheme accounted for more than 4% of CTV traffic observed by HUMAN, using compromised Android TV boxes to impersonate legitimate streaming apps and generate advertising activity without viewers’ knowledge.

The Nov. 18 disclosure raises fresh questions about the effectiveness of CTV ad fraud detection — and how much fraudulent inventory slips through existing safeguards, important gaps for the industry to collectively plug as marketers increasingly spend ad dollars on such channels.

According to HUMAN’s Satori Threat Intelligence team, the situation involved a network of compromised, low-cost Android-based streaming devices running malware designed to generate fraudulent video advertising activity without their owners’ knowledge.

The operation was more than three times larger, by peak daily bid-request volume, than VASTFLUX, previously the largest publicly disclosed scheme measured on that basis.

Researchers linked elements of the malware distribution infrastructure to TXCZ, a Chinese electronics manufacturer, identifying connections involving device software, code repositories and command-and-control servers.

HUMAN also uncovered links to earlier BADBOX operations, including BADBOX 2.0, which was exposed in 2025 and involved more than 10 million compromised devices across 222 countries and territories.

The latest discovery illustrates how fraud operations can reconstitute themselves following earlier disruptions, adapting their infrastructure and techniques to evade detection.

The malware then installed advertising software on infected devices, allowing video commercials to play in hidden windows while users continued watching television or navigating their streaming interfaces.

The resulting advertising requests impersonated legitimate CTV applications, making the inventory appear authentic to downstream buyers.

Some fraudulent requests also originated from residential proxy networks, helping disguise their source as ordinary household internet traffic.

HUMAN identified 11 proxy networks in which compromised devices could be enrolled without their owners’ consent, effectively turning consumer internet connections into infrastructure available for third-party use. Separately, researchers uncovered spoofed server-side ad insertion traffic, in which fraudulent requests purported to represent advertisements inserted into streaming sessions that did not actually exist.

The scale of the operation is considerable, although its financial impact remains unclear.

Crucially, the 40 billion figure represents bid requests, not completed advertising transactions or billable impressions. Consequently, it cannot be used to calculate advertiser losses without establishing how much fraudulent inventory was purchased.

Hence, the question remains: what proportion of the 40 billion daily bid requests became paid impressions? And how much money was spent on invalid inventory?

However, due to the intricacies of online ad auctions – where CPMs can vary significantly – HUMAN was unable to provide an exact dollar amount when asked about the financial impact of the operation.

Nonetheless, sources approached by Digiday estimated that BADBOX 3.0 could potentially have cost advertisers millions of dollars per day at its height.

Shailin Dhar, partner at Futureproof TMT, cautioned against equating the operation’s 40 billion daily bid requests with actual advertiser losses, noting that CTV supply audited by his firm since 2024 has averaged a fill rate of approximately 2%. He further counseled that fraudulent inventory originating from low-end applications and devices could perform considerably worse.

At this juncture, it’s worth considering that enormous volumes of fraudulent auction traffic do not necessarily translate into equivalent volumes of wasted advertising expenditure. At an illustrative fill rate of 0.5% and realized revenue of $3 per thousand impressions, 40 billion daily requests would generate approximately $600,000 in revenue. However, Dhar stressed that such calculations should not be mistaken for evidence of the operation’s actual earnings.

Nevertheless, the operation’s ability to masquerade as legitimate streaming inventory highlights potential weaknesses in how CTV advertising transactions are authenticated.

CTV has become an increasingly important channel for advertisers seeking to reach audiences migrating from traditional television. However, its programmatic infrastructure also presents opportunities for fraudsters to exploit fragmented supply paths and inconsistent verification practices.

BADBOX 3.0 demonstrates how apparently legitimate app identifiers, residential IP addresses and video ad requests can be combined to manufacture the appearance of genuine viewing activity. The question is whether existing safeguards can consistently identify such behavior before advertisers are charged.

Futureproof’s Dhar questioned the effectiveness of existing verification safeguards, arguing that private marketplaces and curated deals remain vulnerable because of limited device, content, and connection signals, alongside excessive confidence in identity matching.

“My personal estimate is roughly a 90% chance that at least one comparable operation is running without public identification,” he told Digiday, while acknowledging that its scale and financial impact remain unknown.

Per Dhar’s assessment, effective CTV verification requires persistent checks throughout the advertising supply chain, rather than relying exclusively on pre-bid or post-bid detection.

For now, HUMAN says customers using its Ad Fraud Defense service are protected against the operation’s associated attacks, while its researchers continue monitoring the perpetrators for further adaptations.

The findings come roughly a month after a separate investigation by ad security firm Confiant and researchers at Citizen Lab exposed how online advertising infrastructure was used to distribute spyware, highlighting another vulnerability in the digital advertising ecosystem.

That investigation, detailed in research published by Citizen Lab, found that Israeli company Discover-Tech exploited targeted advertising mechanisms to deliver zero-click spyware, including attacks against devices at Al Jazeera.

While the two operations differed in their objectives — one targeting advertising budgets, the other facilitating surveillance — both illustrate how infrastructure designed to connect advertisers with audiences can be repurposed for malicious activity.

The broader concern is that BADBOX 3.0 is another iteration of an established threat rather than an isolated incident — and that dismantling one operation does not necessarily eliminate the infrastructure or incentives behind the next.

FutureSight’s new tool can help banks of all sizes get a side-by-side idea of how their media mix stacks up against the competition.

Meta’s reported CTV expansion and AppLovin’s alleged interest in Criteo are foreboding for independent ad tech as major platforms extend their reach.

#7385. Google Adds Pageburst & 11 Other Existing Bots To Its Crawler Docs via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

Google's crawler docs now list pageburst, which renders pages for Google Ads and ignores robots.txt, plus more existing user agents to check in server logs.

Google identified pageburst as a user agent that renders pages to measure Google Ads quality and landing page safety and ignores robots.txt rules. Its two strings look like a browser’s and do not contain “Googlebot”; a bot rule created using “Googlebot” will not capture them.

Pageburst is one of 12 existing user agents Google added to its crawler documentation on Nov. 23, along with a corrected entry for APIs-Google. Google’s crawling documentation changelog explains:

“These crawlers and fetchers are not new; we’re documenting existing high-volume clients that are more likely to show up in server logs and that we’ve received questions about.”

The 12 belong to Google products other than Search, such as Google Ads, Gmail and Google Cloud.

Google’s special-case crawlers page, which lists crawlers used by specific Google products, says pageburst “renders web pages for Google Ads quality, landing-page safety, and page understanding.” The entry adds that “it’s unaffected by crawling preferences.”

The desktop string identifies as Chrome on Linux and the mobile one as Chrome for iOS on an iPad, and both include “compatible; pageburst.”

AdsBot, which checks web page ad quality for Google Ads, has its own robots.txt token. Pageburst’s entry lists no token and says the user agent “ignores robots.txt rules.”

The highlights show what to look for in server logs and where Google states its robots.txt policy.

Google’s documentation says user-agent strings can be faked. Special-case crawlers use the IP addresses defined in Google’s special-crawlers.json; these have a reverse-DNS match of rate-limited-proxy-***-***-***-***.google.com. The pageburst entry does not say what occurs when a website blocks the Google Ads check.

Besides pageburst, each of the five other newly documented special-case entries says the user agent “ignores robots.txt rules.”

Google’s user-triggered fetchers page covers the six newly documented fetchers and says that because a user requested the fetch, these fetchers “generally ignore robots.txt rules.” Three of those (AppEngine-Google, Google-Apps-Script and Google-Cloud-Tasks) send requests for code running within Google’s platform-based products. The remaining three are GoogleImageProxy, which is used to load image content into email applications such as Gmail, along with Google Web Preview and the PageSpeed Insights fetcher, both with strings ending in Chrome-Lighthouse.

Several of the newly listed user agents seem to use standard browser strings. For example, a string from GoogleImageProxy appears similar to Firefox 11 on Windows NT 5.1; the strings for Google Web Preview and PageSpeed Insights, and one of PlayStore-Google’s, were created using Chrome strings. A filter that only identifies “Googlebot” would miss all of these.

Google has moved APIs-Google, which makes requests to the webhook notification systems developers create within Google Cloud and Google Workspace APIs, from the list of special-case crawlers to the list of user-triggered fetchers. APIs-Google’s push requests, the changelog says, “come from the user-triggered fetcher IP ranges and ignore robots.txt rules.” Google added a missing semicolon after “APIs-Google” in its documented string and tells developers to modify any code that was previously using a hardcoded version of the earlier string.

Prior to the Nov. 23 update, Google had included robots.txt as a method to block requests from APIs-Google in its documentation. In an Oct. 21 capture, the robots.txt token was present on the special-case page. On Oct. 30, a capture of the APIs-Google page showed “Use robots.txt” as one of two methods to block requests from APIs-Google. Now the APIs-Google page says that it “ignores robots.txt rules”; for controlling the delivery of notifications, the page points to either the developer who created the notification system or Google Cloud’s abuse form for unexpected requests.

Pageburst renders pages for ads in Google and does not follow robots.txt. Check for “pageburst” in the log entries for your servers and CDNs, verify with Google’s procedures that the IP addresses are in its special-crawler ranges, and see if your pages were delivered to the verified requests, or if a challenge or a 403 was returned.

Roger Montti covered Google’s advice on Nov. 18 that general bot blocking may keep Googlebot from crawling content when moving a CDN; the same advice should be applied to other Google clients that do not have the name Googlebot.

Google’s special-case and user-triggered pages both say their lists aren’t exhaustive and cover the requestors “more likely to show up in log files.” The crawling documentation changelog, which is where Google logs additions like these, has an RSS feed.

#7383. Pinterest simplifies parental controls

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The platform has updated its parental control dashboard to offer a more streamlined way to manage devices and access options.

Pinterest has updated its parental control elements to offer a more integrated, streamlined process and make it easier for parents to manage their child’s in-app experience.

As shown in these example screens, Pinterest’s updated parental controls dashboard now includes all of the app’s oversight and management options in one place, including profile visibility, content recommendations and connection controls.

The updated parental controls also include direct links to manage device-level screen time and location settings. Parents will also be able to make their kids’ profiles private by default and set limits on ad personalization and social features.

In addition, Pinterest added tools that allow parents to control the amount of artificial intelligence-generated content that teens see in the app. There’s also new notification management functionality.

Parents can also decide whether their teens have autoplay video switched on or not, which could help to combat compulsive viewing behaviors.

Pinterest has been working to present its app as an alternative to potentially harmful, engagement-focused approaches that have been adopted by other social media platforms.

In September, Pinterest published a report on how teens use the app, which showed that more than 77% of its teen audience uses Pinterest to explore creative interests.

More teen control options will provide additional peace of mind for parents, which could help to further establish Pinterest as a safer space for young users.

#7382. OpenAI Isn’t Planning Prompt-Level Reports For ChatGPT Ads via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

ChatGPT ads match to queries OpenAI's own system writes. Advertisers can't see them, and OpenAI says prompt-level reports aren't planned. Here's what it means.

OpenAI doesn’t plan to provide ChatGPT advertisers with reports showing the prompts or inferred intent behind their ads. When Adweek asked whether advertisers could expect such reports, Vijaye Raji, OpenAI’s CTO of applications, said they should not expect them.

Three executives who run OpenAI’s ad system told Adweek that ChatGPT ads are matched to search queries written by the company’s own AI agent. Advertisers don’t see those queries, only aggregate results.

OpenAI’s basics page for advertisers explains that Ads Manager Beta reporting currently includes impressions, clicks, spend, CTR, average CPC, average CPM and conversions.

OpenAI’s “About this ad” panel tells users why they saw an ad and what performance data advertisers receive.

OpenAI’s ad system begins by creating one or more search queries based upon buying intent determined from the conversation, per the company’s ads engineering post published Oct. 21 by Ritendra Datta and Karthik Gopalratnam. OpenAI calls the model that creates these search queries the orchestrator. Using these search queries, the ad system retrieves candidate ads, filters them, scores them and identifies the top candidates to be entered into an auction to set the price and select the winner. Returning no ad is called “an ordinary, successful outcome” in the post.

As described in the post, if a user asks about a two-day Yosemite trip and then about a shoe brand’s new product lines, the ad system may create a query representing that conversation such as “shoes appropriate for hiking trip,” even though the user did not connect the two questions.

According to the post, when ads personalization is turned on, the orchestrator will also consider “nonsensitive information about the user’s past conversations.”

ChatGPT users in the European Economic Area and Switzerland will not have access to personalized ads at first, according to OpenAI’s ads FAQ for users. Brooke Osmundson covered the engineering post in October.

Advertisers share context hints about where an ad might fit, and OpenAI says these hints help guide matching without determining it.

“Hints are not targeting rules or delivery instructions. They do not guarantee that your ad will appear for particular conversations, audiences, or situations, and they cannot enforce geographic limits, schedules, or exclusions.”

The basics page also says that hints “are not exact-match keywords.” Negative Phrases help qualifying advertisers limit where their ads appear, for “narrow placement requirements specific to their brand’s own policies.” The option is not necessarily available to every advertiser.

Google explains that for some AI searches, the search terms provided in Google Ads reporting reflect the user’s intent rather than the exact query. According to Google’s ad group prioritization page, for searches done through Lens, AI Mode, AI Overviews and autocomplete, “the search term shown in your reporting represents the best approximation of the user’s intent.” Brooke posted about Google’s update to that page in May.

OpenAI does not list a search terms report on its basics page.

ChatGPT advertisers can determine what a campaign delivered, but they cannot see the conversations or queries that led to the results. Click-based and conversion-based campaigns can use the conversion tracking OpenAI supports through Ads Manager Beta. The basics page also describes how UTM parameters added to landing page URLs persist on ad clicks.

OpenAI recommends writing your context hints in terms of customer needs and scenarios instead of listing keywords. Also, use OpenAI’s product controls where available to restrict delivery by geography.

#7379. D+ Research: Brand’s holiday marketing tactics shift in 2026

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

This research is based on unique data collected from our proprietary audience of publisher, agency, brand and tech insiders. It’s available to Digiday+ members. More from the series →

This is an excerpt from our Digiday+ Research report The 2026 guide to holiday marketing strategies, including A-Frame Brands, Mastercard and Ritual, which examined which commerce channels are dominating marketers’ holiday strategies. The report is based on a survey of 90 brand and retailer professionals, as well as individual interviews with marketing executives.

Digiday’s survey found that brands and retailers plan to adjust the marketing tactics they’ll use during the 2026 holiday season in comparison to those they used in 2025.

The biggest changes are that CTV/streaming and TV ads are gaining traction in 2026, with year-over-year increases of 22 percentage points and 20 percentage points, respectively.

Forty-five percent of survey respondents said they plan to use CTV/streaming ads this holiday season, in comparison to 23% of respondents who said the same in 2025. The 2026 uptick followed a 14 percentage point dip in usage from 2024 to 2025.Meanwhile, marketers’ usage of TV ads remained relatively stable between 2024 and 2025, dropping by only 4 percentage points between 2024 and 2025, but grew by a whopping 20 percentage points in 2026. Thirty-three percent of brands and retailers said they plan to use TV ads this holiday season in comparison to 13% of marketers who said the same in 2025.

“Streaming is a really valid channel to invest in during holiday because consumption of that media spikes,” said Laura Brodie, chief growth officer at supplement company Ritual. “But participating in streaming is actually a decision for the whole year. Starting to engage just for holiday would be a risky move, especially for a smaller brand.”

“If you have the data to back it up over the course of the year showing this is a channel that’s proven and the ROI metrics associated, it can make a lot of sense to spike it during holiday,” she added.

Ari Bloom, founder and CEO of brand incubator A-Frame Brands, said that both streaming and TV ads can be effective for targeting specific demographic groups during the holidays. “Streaming and television is an effective audience conversion mechanism, especially with women over 30 years old,” Bloom said. “We’ve done a lot of work on daytime TV and on QVC. We see significantly bigger segments in the holiday time period from November through mid-December, and we always put attention on those times.”

Last year, brands’ and retailers’ most-used holiday marketing tactic was brand experiences, but that strategy fell to second place in 2026 behind streaming/CTV ads. Forty-one percent of marketers said they expect to use brand experiences as a marketing strategy during the 2026 holiday season in comparison to 50% of marketers who said the same in 2025 — a drop of 9 percentage points.

Brands and retailers are also divesting from using gift guides and influencer hauls/unboxing videos this holiday season. Marketers’ usage of gift guides decreased by 19 percentage points in 2026 vs. 2025, while their use of influencer hauls/unboxing videos fell by 14 percentage points this year in comparison to last year.

Although gift guides and brand experiences decreased in marketer usage for the 2026 holidays, they remain brands’ and retailers’ top performing holiday marketing tactics over time. Thirty-one percent of marketers said gift guides have historically performed the best for their company during the holiday season, while 28% of marketers said the same of brand experiences, putting them in the No. 1 and No. 2 ranking spots, respectively.

Although some marketers are shifting away from using gift guides for the upcoming holiday season, Ritual’s Brodie said gift guides are likely to gain importance in the AI-driven search era because AI-powered search tools often rely on best of lists and curated recommendations to answer consumer queries.

“Gift guides are very interesting in the world of AEO and thinking about LLM optimization,” Brodie said. “Overall, best of lists and gift guides are a close sister to [AI search results]. Gift guides can play an important role in holiday and especially bridging LLM research and AI overviews. So, I’m bullish about gift guides.”

Although brands and retailers are leaning into CTV/streaming ads for the 2026 holidays, those marketing tactics tied in the No. 4 spot for the best-performing holiday marketing tactic over time, while pop-up shops ranked No. 3. Influencer hauls/unboxing videos was the only marketing strategy that fell in both best historic performance and marketers’ intended use during the 2026 holiday season.

A-Frame Brands’ Bloom said brands and retailers should also consider investing in catalogs for the 2026 holiday. “Catalogs have always been very successful, and they’re heavily conversion-focused,” Bloom explained. “When they’re discount-driven and when people’s attention is on buying, you can do offers that you can only get via physical paper, and it does drive people into stores.”

As social trends accelerate, brands like General Mills are scoring creator posts for shareability to bridge the gap between organic buzz and paid media.

Dick’s is betting that youth sports can fuel its next phase of ad growth through GameChanger—if it can overcome limits on scale.

As Black Friday Cyber Monday rapidly approaches, brands are most focused on acquiring new customers this holiday season.

#7376. Agencies are selling AI efficiency — clients want outcomes

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

Amol Waishampayan, co-founder, fullthrottle.ai

Agencies spent the last two years pitching AI to clients as a cost story. Faster work, leaner teams, lower fees. Clients took the meeting, nodded along and then waited for the invoice to shrink. It didn’t. AI strategies now sound interchangeable to clients, who say the savings never showed up in their fees.

That is not an AI problem. It is a positioning problem. Efficiency was the wrong promise. Clients do not hire agencies to be fast. They hire them to grow the business. AI’s real opportunity for agencies is not doing the same work cheaper. It is doing work that actually moves revenue, and proving it.

Agencies are getting operational value from AI. According to the Digiday Media Agency Report 2026, 70% of agencies say AI has cut costs by making tasks more efficient, while 31% say it cost more to implement than expected. But efficiency is a one-time gain.

Once every agency has it, nobody gets paid for it. As one Gartner analyst told Digiday, the honeymoon between agencies and AI is “essentially over.” The agencies that build their AI story on productivity are competing on margin. The ones that build it on performance are competing on value, and value is what clients renew.

Most media plans are still organized by channel. Search budget here, social budget there, streaming over in a separate deck. AI makes that structure obsolete, because it can plan around the customer instead.

Take a regional home services company running paid search and social. Those campaigns are producing something more valuable than clicks: a live stream of households actively researching its services. AI can turn those signals into a defined first-party audience, figure out where else those households spend their time, and extend the plan into streaming TV, digital video and audio to reach them there. One audience, coordinated across channels, built from the client’s own demand rather than a platform’s inventory.

That is a different kind of planning. The question stops being “what should we spend on CTV” and becomes “who are we trying to reach, and where are they?”

The next step is letting AI act on that intelligence. Agentic systems can take audience and performance signals and adjust targeting, channel mix and spend as conditions change, instead of waiting for the monthly optimization meeting. Static plans with quarterly reviews are a relic of how long it used to take humans to read the data.

But here is where agencies should be careful. The advantage is not how much of the buying you automate. Anyone can automate. The advantage is whether the agent is optimizing toward something that matters. An agent chasing cheaper CPMs will find them, and the client will not care. An agent optimizing toward the client’s actual business outcomes, with the agency keeping full transparency and control, is a different product entirely.

This is the part most of the industry still avoids. Clicks and impressions are easy to report and nearly impossible to defend in a budget conversation. The only metrics a CFO cares about are sales, customers and revenue.

Once that loop exists, everything upstream improves. Planning gets smarter because it is fed by real conversions. Agentic buying gets better because it is optimizing toward revenue instead of proxies. And the agency walks into every renewal with proof rather than a deck.

Agencies are already monetizing AI. Digiday’s report found that 59% are launching new AI-powered products, 34% are selling strategic roadmaps or audits and 31% are charging additional fees for AI-powered services. But if the product is “we have AI,” the pricing power will not last. Every competitor has AI. Within a year, every client will have it too.

The agencies that win the next cycle will not be the ones with the most AI. They will be the ones who can show a client exactly what it delivered, in the client’s own numbers. Efficiency gets agencies a thank-you. Outcomes get agencies the next three years of the account.Partner insights from fullthrottle.ai

#7372. Campaign Trail: Tiffany tells human holiday story with Hollywood talent

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The luxury brand and agency American Haiku leaned into real emotions with actor Amanda Seyfried and director Derek Cianfrance.

In adland, it has been a decidedly handmade holiday season, with brands including Levi’s and E.l.f. turning to techniques like stop-motion animation to connect with consumers who are growing weary of ads created by artificial intelligence.

For its annual holiday effort, Tiffany & Co. found the best way to resonate with consumers is through human storytelling. The luxury brand’s global campaign, “Love is a Gift,” was created with agency American Haiku and revolves around a two-minute film starring actor Amanda Seyfried and director Derek Cianfrance.

The short, “You & Me,” jumps from the present day to New York City in the 1990s to tell the story of a young girl and her mother, played by Seyfried. The girl watches her mother work as a choreographer and has a handful of holiday experiences before being gifted with a Tiffany ornament that she shares with her own daughter in the present.

“Moving between past and present, the film reflects the enduring place Tiffany & Co. holds in life’s most meaningful moments and the stories we carry forward,” said CMO Andrea Davey in a statement.

The film is soundtracked by a cover of The Wannadies’ “You & Me Song,” a tune best known for its appearance on the 1996 “Romeo + Juliet” soundtrack. The campaign will run across cinema, paid and organic social, digital out-of-home, owned channels and clienteling across global channels.

Along with being on-trend with regard to stories imbued with humanity, Tiffany’s holiday campaign also represents a pivot from the brand’s past holiday creative. The 2025 edition of the “Love is a Gift” campaign turned its iconic blue boxes into portals to love stories around the world. This year, Tiffany brought on American Haiku, which had worked on a previous campaign for the brand in the U.K., but didn’t offer a traditional brief.

“They came to us with an initial idea of a family spending the holidays in their home and [tapping] into the memory aspect,” said Ben Muckensturm, creative director at the shop. “Where we pushed the work was bringing in the importance of the mother-daughter relationship that I think is the core of the story.”

Keying into the mother-daughter story gave the brand and agency a larger insight around the memory of seeing a parent as a person in their own world that is relatable to consumers, whether or not they are wealthy residents of the Upper East Side like the characters in the film. In the film, the true gift is not the ornament but the memory that is associated with it.

“That opened us up to how we explore the past and then bring it back to the present and create a piece that feels essentially real, that anyone could connect with,” Muckensturm said. “Everything was shot in New York. It was definitely an intentional push to try to bring it to the real world and make it more of an emotional piece.”

“You & Me” also delivers nostalgia for a pre-digital ‘90s that has been a reliable way to engage millennial audiences. However, the nostalgia in the film is not the traditional touchstones, like technology and boy bands, used by marketers looking to tap into memories of the decade. Instead, Tiffany looked at its own archives and at the holidays of movies like “Home Alone” and “The Parent Trap” for inspiration.

“When we created the town house, we went back to old archival Tiffany imagery of how things were,” Muckensturm said of creating the main set for the ad. “Especially on Fifth Avenue, most of the references that we brought were from ‘Home Alone 2,’ like what the streets looked like at the time. It's great to be able to tap into things that people are familiar with.”

After creating the world of the ad, the agency populated it with brand ambassador Seyfried, whose character is the mother in the past, rather than the main character in the present-day framing device. The actor, an Academy Award nominee whose performance in one of the year’s biggest films has captivated audiences, brought her gifts to the production.

“She has such a maternal instinct that really played perfectly on set, and you could see really how she was a mother to that girl for the days that we shot,” Muckensturm said.

The choice of Cianfrance, a director best known for dramatic fare like “Blue Valentine” and “The Place Beyond the Pines,” helped the brand and agency get the emotional tone right, without rehearsal and without falling into familiar or even corny holiday tropes.

“There was a trusting relationship between production partners, us and the client to come into it with a really open mind to see what the scene gives us,” Muckensturm said. “We knew where we were going to shoot, and we were trying to get a range of emotion… but we really let him direct them and let this play naturally.”

#7370. Meta launches iPad version of Edits

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The larger screen layout is intended to make it easier for users to manage video projects.

Meta has launched an iPad version of its Edits video editing app, while it's also added new tools and effects, as it continues to expand its video creation options.

The iPad launch will enable tablet users to edit their video clips on a larger screen.

As shown in this example screen, Edits for iPad has a bigger composition screen, which will make it easier to hone in on specific elements and access more editing options at one time.

It could be a valuable update for video creators. A MacOS version of Edits, which is the first desktop version of the app, launched earlier this month.

Edits also added a trim-upon-import option, which should make it easier to place clips into a project at the exact right time.

While it also added new filters and 1,600 new stickers. It's also experimenting with LUT file import options.

LUT files enable color conversion within video files, and this addition will provide more options in maintaining video style and format in the app.

Meta also expanded Edits’ artificial intelligence assistant capacity, with users now able to upload images and video into the chat and get recommendations on how to create a video from these sources.

Finally, there’s a new copyright check option in Edits on iOS, which will examine video projects for potential copyright concerns before they’re uploaded.

As shown in this image posted on X by app researcher Radu Oncescu, users will have five copyright checks available per day, which should help to avoid any restrictions or penalties.

These new tools expand the functionality of Edits and should provide more ways to build creative projects in the app.

#7369. The next test for agentic media

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

Anudit Vikram, Chief Product Officer, Channel Factory

Advertisers are building AI systems around the way their teams already work. These teams have their own agents, their own data and their own rules for what an agent may and may not do. At the same time, most of the specialized intelligence they depend on still sits inside separate vendor platforms.

As a result, vendor intelligence shapes a recommendation while remaining disconnected from the system acting on the recommendation. When planners carry conclusions between tools, the evidence and conditions behind those recommendations often fall away.

That’s the problem agentic media has to solve next. Can the intelligence behind the agent go where the work happens?

Models and agent frameworks are widely available. Two vendors can build on the same foundation and ship agents that look identical in a demo. What separates them is what the agent knows, and whether the advertiser can put that knowledge to work. In media buying, that knowledge is specific.

A broad content classification offers only a starting point for a media decision. Suitability depends on the particular advertiser and market, and those judgments can change quickly when breaking news alters the significance of a placement. A general-purpose model can’t reconstruct that brand-specific knowledge or historical context from a prompt alone. Classification depth and performance history can.

For Channel Factory, that means IAB 3.0 classification across more than 15 million YouTube channels, and more than 10 years and $4 billion of campaign performance data. To be clear, this isn’t an argument for keeping that intelligence locked inside a platform; it’s the opposite. Intelligence that only works inside its owner’s interface is as limited as a capable agent no one can reach.

So the test is portability. Can an advertiser’s own agent call on a provider’s intelligence directly, from inside the planning and buying environment it already uses? That’s how Channel Factory is building, with contextual and suitability intelligence made available through APIs and MCP servers, and delivered through modular agents that run inside an advertiser’s environment or alongside it.

With this architecture, market-specific suitability analysis becomes part of an advertiser’s own planning process. An agent can evaluate inventory against the provider’s classifications and historical performance data, applying the relevant standards for each market. Those findings can directly inform the plan, with the advertiser’s existing rules governing what the agent can recommend or change.

Portable intelligence doesn’t mean identical agents. Two advertisers can draw on the same underlying intelligence and make different decisions. For instance, one avoids content when signals are unclear while another favors reaching inside defined boundaries. Both are valid because the thresholds, priorities and approval rules are the advertisers’.

An agent’s knowledge source shouldn’t determine the scope of its authority. The brand decides what acceptable judgment looks like. The provider keeps the classification, history and models current.

Learning needs the same discipline. Feedback and outcomes should refine recommendations, but advertisers should decide what shapes future decisions and which policies stay fixed. On its own, a successful campaign shouldn’t rewrite a brand’s suitability standards.

Intelligence that moves into someone else’s systems has to carry its accountability along. As agents shift from recommending to acting, teams need to see what changed, why and whether it stayed within approved limits.

The principle is simple: Agents do the reasoning, and the engine owns the state, so every action is authorized, logged and traceable to the signals behind it. People define the strategy. Autonomy is earned in stages: alerts first, then recommendations, then bounded actions. An agent might make a small budget adjustment under set conditions while sending a larger change for human approval. How much authority to delegate is the advertiser’s call, and the system should make that call easy to enforce and easy to review.

As agentic capabilities spread, feature lists will converge. Advertisers should look underneath the interface and put three questions to any provider:

The providers who can answer those clearly will matter more as brands take greater control of how they buy media. The rest will be unrealized demos.

As social trends accelerate, brands like General Mills are scoring creator posts for shareability to bridge the gap between organic buzz and paid media.

Dick’s is betting that youth sports can fuel its next phase of ad growth through GameChanger—if it can overcome limits on scale.

As Black Friday Cyber Monday rapidly approaches, brands are most focused on acquiring new customers this holiday season.

#7368. How Jell-O’s new creative platform looks to shift consumer perceptions

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The campaign, the first by Johannes Leonardo for the Kraft Heinz brand, represents its largest marketing investment in more than a decade.

Jell-O on Monday launched a new creative platform, “Oh Hello, Jell-O,” that seeks to shift consumer perceptions about how the product can be enjoyed beyond traditional use cases. The effort represents the Kraft Heinz brand’s largest marketing investment in more than a decade, per details shared with Marketing Dive.

“As a nearly 130-year-old brand, we recognized a disconnect between how familiar consumers are with Jell-O and how often they think to purchase it,” Kathryn O’Brien, head of marketing for desserts at Kraft Heinz, said in emailed comments. “We want Jell-O to be more than something that comes to mind for a bowl of gelatin or pudding, but rather a part of the creative process in the kitchen.”

Central to the campaign are two 15-second spots that show home cooks in monochrome kitchens preparing desserts with Jell-O before a social-inspired flip transition pivots the scene to others marveling over the finished product.

The campaign was created by Johannes Leonardo and is the first campaign for the brand by the agency, which has held creative duties on select Kraft Heinz brands since 2020. The spots were directed by Drew Kirsch, a veteran of music videos who has worked with Taylor Swift, and feature an original electronic-pop song that uses “oh hello, Jell-O” as a vocal hook.

“Rather than borrowing an existing song, we saw an opportunity to build an ownable sonic identity around the platform,” O’Brien said. “The original track is a recognizable brand asset that can extend across social, content and future campaign moments.”

As part of the launch, Jell-O will take over the Las Vegas Sphere this week, transforming the orb into a gelatin mold, a “dirt cup” dessert and banana cream pudding. “Oh Hello, Jell-O” will run across streaming, online video, social and digital throughout 2027, with investment pulsing around key seasonal moments. The significant media investment comes at a pivotal moment for the brand, O’Brien explained.

“Our first-ever CTV buy allows us to bring the campaign's highly visual, music-driven creative to life on the big screen, showcasing the playfulness, vibrant colors and unexpected transformations in a high-attention environment,” the executive said. “We're taking an integrated approach throughout 2027, combining streaming and online video with social, digital and e-commerce touchpoints.”

The creative platform builds on a 2023 rebrand, crafted with agency Brand Opus, that updated Jell-O’s visual identity with a more modern look and feel. The rebrand, which at the time was its first such effort in 10 years, arrived amid an industry-wide move to help CPG brands engage with new consumer groups.

Kraft Heinz in February stopped plans to split its condiment and grocery staples businesses, with CEO Steve Cahillane saying many of the CPG company’s challenges are fixable. The company is pouring $700 million into a turnaround strategy that includes significant investments in marketing, which has been increased to at least 6% of net sales.

While Kraft Heinz saw organic net sales decrease 1.1% in Q3 2026, the company’s market share, sales and volume trends improved in every region, per an earnings report. Jell-O was cited on an earnings call as a brand with which the company is looking to win share by investing selectively.

#7366. Amazon is buying ChatGPT ads while blocking OpenAI crawlers

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

Amazon is paying OpenAI to reach the same shoppers it refuses to let ChatGPT study.

After a relatively quiet few months on the chatbot following its Prime Day activity, the e-commerce giant has returned to the platform with a new round of Black Friday ads in the U.S., Digiday has seen.

The ads, which are the same format as typical ChatGPT ads — separate from the user conversation, with a favicon, headline, description and a “Learn more” call to action — are appearing in ChatGPT in the lead-up to Black Friday. They promote Amazon Black Friday deals and direct users to Amazon to complete their purchases.

What’s different compared to other retailers, though, is how ChatGPT is surfacing Amazon products and deals. Rather than directing users to individual product pages, ChatGPT’s shopping experience is linking to Amazon search results, while drawing on third-party deal-tracking websites to identify products, discounts and up-to-date pricing. That means ChatGPT can help consumers discover Amazon products and compare deals without necessarily accessing Amazon’s own website directly.

Amazon’s increased activity on ChatGPT is interesting given the retailer already operates its own shopping ecosystem and one of the world’s largest ad businesses. Its presence on the chatbot puts it in the position of using a competing platform to drive shoppers back to its own marketplace, while that same platform is developing its own way of facilitating product discovery around Amazon’s catalogue.

Amazon also has an opportunity to monetize that traffic once shoppers arrive on its marketplace.

“Sending shoppers to Amazon search results rather than individual product pages also creates another opportunity to make money from advertising,” said Arielle Feger, senior analyst, commerce media and retail at eMarketer.

Amazon’s U.S. search ad revenues are forecasted to reach $40.57 billion this year, nearly a quarter of all U.S. search ad spending. Traffic coming from ChatGPT gives Amazon another opportunity to put sponsored products in front of shoppers.

“For brands, that creates a risk of paying twice for the same customer,” Feger added. “Even after winning a recommendation in ChatGPT, a brand could find itself paying again to compete against sponsored listings on Amazon.”

But Amazon’s relationship with ChatGPT extends beyond buying ad space for its own products.

In September, Amazon Ads announced a partnership with OpenAI that allows advertisers to buy ChatGPT inventory through Amazon’s DSP, extending their existing Amazon ad campaigns onto the chatbot. The integration initially gives select U.S. advertisers access to ChatGPT’s ad inventory through Amazon DSP, giving brands another route to reach consumers using the AI chatbot.

What is unclear is whether Amazon has bought its ChatGPT ads directly from OpenAI, or through its own DSP.

Both Amazon and OpenAI declined to comment on this article.

As social trends accelerate, brands like General Mills are scoring creator posts for shareability to bridge the gap between organic buzz and paid media.

Dick’s is betting that youth sports can fuel its next phase of ad growth through GameChanger—if it can overcome limits on scale.

As Black Friday Cyber Monday rapidly approaches, brands are most focused on acquiring new customers this holiday season.

#7364. Meta says social media is key driver for holiday discovery

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

People who shop via social media are more likely to purchase across multiple categories and self-gift, according to the company.

Meta’s has shared some key data notes on shopping activity in its apps, which could provide additional guidance for brands to assist with their holiday campaign planning.

The data was published earlier this year, and is based on research conducted by Ipsos, which surveyed 14,473 shoppers in 18 countries across North America, Latin America, Europe and Asia-Pacific.

The data found that social media is a key driver of discovery for holiday season shoppers.

As per Meta: “Across all 18 markets surveyed, 37% of festive shoppers use social media for gift discovery and inspiration. That places it on par with search engines (41%) and ahead of TV advertising (27%).”

The data also showed that video is the most influential content type, while high-quality product photography is also a valuable driver.

The report also looked at what drives purchase decisions among social media shoppers.

While it also explored key spending behaviors.

As per the report: “Social shoppers are far more commercially engaged than the average holiday shopper. They plan to spend more (49% intend to increase spending year-on-year, compared to 36% overall), shop across more product categories (5.4 vs 4.3 average) and are more likely to self-gift (83% vs 67%).”

There’s also insight into how shoppers use messaging apps, and what they’re looking for in brand DMs.

Based on these insights, Meta advised marketers to invest in discovery on social platforms, and to use customer endorsements and testimonials to assure potential customers of their quality.

Meta also said that marketers should design their campaigns for cross-category shoppers: “Use consistent creative systems and shoppable catalogues to reduce the friction between ‘that looks interesting’ and ‘I'm buying this’.”

These notes could help to refine holiday campaign approaches.

Rather than only showing the product as a cold spread for bagels and snacks, the platform highlights how cream cheese can be used to enrich more involved meals. In the new work, Phillyboy acts as a Santa-like figure, trotting into houses saddled on his dairy cow to dole out blocks of cream cheese that are then used to make cheesecake. #7361. Ad Tech Briefing: Meta eyes CTV as AppLovin circles Criteo, signs of the squeeze on independent ad tech

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

This Ad Tech Briefing covers the latest in ad tech and platforms for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Tuesday at 10 a.m. ET. More from the series →

AppLovin’s reported interest in Criteo and Meta’s plans to explore CTV could put further pressure on independent ad tech, with some companies reporting challenging circumstances in the latest round of earnings calls.

Last week, Reuters reported unconfirmed acquisition discussions involving AppLovin and Criteo, the same day Next in Media reported that Meta was exploring partnerships with television manufacturers and free FAST services to extend its advertising platform into CTV.

If both sets of developments materialize, it would represent two of the largest established (mobile) ad platforms expanding into new channels using existing advertiser relationships, data, and buying technology.

It’s well understood that AppLovin wants to extend its performance advertising business beyond mobile applications, and Criteo — a company that is reportedly seeking an exit from the public markets — could provide retail relationships, commerce data, and access to advertisers across the open web.

Meanwhile, Meta could use its existing buying platform to help advertisers reach television audiences without relying on a separate demand-side platform.

In recent weeks, separate sources told Digiday this could prove a key advantage in helping the social networking outfit eat into Google’s lead in markets where its DSP, DV 360, dominates.

However, developments could reduce advertisers’ dependence on independent DSPs and supply-side platforms.

AppLovin’s potential shortcut into commerce

Private equity firms Vista Equity Partners and Quinti Capital have also reportedly expressed interest in Criteo, which has engaged an investment bank to evaluate its options.

AppLovin reported third-quarter revenue of $2.19 billion, up 55% year over year, alongside $1.44 billion in net income.

Criteo reported a 12% revenue decline to $416 million, with net income falling to approximately $6 million.

AppLovin’s growth has been driven by mobile advertising, although the company is increasingly targeting e-commerce advertisers outside of gaming.

Criteo has spent years expanding beyond retargeting into commerce media, developing relationships with retailers, access to shopper data and cross-channel advertising capabilities.

Per official figures, Criteo’s commerce intelligence draws on more than $1 trillion in annual transactions, 740 million daily active users and over 5 billion product SKUs, and acquiring it could accelerate AppLovin’s expansion into retail media, providing relationships and data it would otherwise need to develop independently.

However, integrating the businesses would be complicated given that AppLovin’s core technology is built around mobile apps, while Criteo operates across retailers, publishers, and other commerce environments.

The potential benefits would depend on whether their different data assets, buying systems, and commercial relationships could work effectively when integrated.

Earlier in the year, multiple sources told Digiday that Meta is ⁠exploring an option that would allow advertisers to extend campaigns into third-party television inventory through its existing advertising tools — a measurement tactic commonly known as audience extension.

The latest reporting suggests Meta is considering how those relationships could support an advertiser-facing buying option, resembling Pinterest’s CTV audience-extension offering, which lets advertisers use Pinterest’s audience data to reach consumers beyond its owned properties. Meta could pursue a similar approach at considerably greater scale.

Its existing advertiser base could access television inventory without establishing separate relationships with specialist CTV buying platforms, an attractive option for smaller advertisers already using Meta’s automated campaign tools.

For DSPs and SSPs, the competitive implications would be significant, as Meta could bring more advertisers directly into CTV, potentially reducing the role of intermediaries that connect buyers with television inventory.

But questions remain about how the proposed model would operate. For example, would Meta determine which inventory advertisers purchase? Plus, how would fees and media costs be disclosed? And what independent measurement would be available?

Such details are likely to determine whether Meta’s proposed offering creates a meaningful alternative to existing CTV buying arrangements or simply adds another layer between advertisers and publishers.

AppLovin’s interest in Criteo and Meta’s reported CTV expansion reflect a broader shift in advertising technology, as larger companies with bigger advertiser bases and proprietary data extend their buying capabilities into additional channels. Amazon is pursuing a similar strategy through its DSP and retail media business, which is morphing into a unified agentic platform.

The Trade Desk’s recent financial performance illustrates the difficulties facing some independent players. The company reported a 0.5% third-quarter revenue decline to $736 million, marking a rare contraction after years of sustained growth, and is on course to simplify and offer new measurement capabilities as it attempts to restore growth.

While The Trade Desk’s recent revenue decline cannot be attributed to Meta’s reported plans or AppLovin’s potential acquisition, the contrast provides context for broader competitive pressure on independent buying platforms.

The emergence of unified media platforms is another response, as ⁠last week’s explainer outlined; these systems aim to coordinate advertising across search, social, programmatic, and direct publisher relationships.

But coordinating buying across platforms is not the same as controlling the underlying inventory, data, or optimization technology. Independent companies will need to demonstrate value beyond simplifying workflows, particularly as AI makes campaign execution easier.

For independent ad tech, maintaining a meaningful role in that environment will become increasingly difficult.

Figures from ⁠HUMAN Security’s BADBOX 3.0 investigation, published Nov. 18.

#7360. YouTube enables custom Shorts thumbnails

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

All users can now add custom thumbnails for their Shorts clips.

After initially telling creators that Shorts thumbnails were not particularly important for discovery, YouTube has reversed course and has now enabled Shorts thumbnail customization options for all creators.

As shown in this example screen, which was posted by YouTube CEO Neal Mohan on X, creators can upload a custom thumbnail image in YouTube Studio’s Shorts flow.

YouTube’s head of editorial Rene Ritchie explained that creators on mobile or desktop can upload a thumbnail image at the upload stage, while they can also change the video thumbnail after publishing.

“If you don’t want a custom image for your thumbnail, you can pick from a suggested frame from the Short to use as the thumbnail,” Ritchie added.

Ritchie also said creators can use YouTube’s artificial intelligence-powered Ask Studio assistant to brainstorm thumbnail ideas.

Shorts thumbnails were initially made available to creators in the YouTube Partner Program in June, with YouTube then gradually expanding access to the option over time.

Many creators have been asking for Shorts thumbnails, but initially YouTube wasn’t planning to add them at all.

In 2024, YouTube said that Shorts thumbnails were not as important as regular video thumbnail images because most users come across Shorts clips when they’re scrolling through full-screen video displays, as opposed to tapping on a smaller thumbnail to activate a Shorts clip.

Eventually, YouTube added in Shorts thumbnail customization anyway, and this latest update is the final step in enabling Shorts thumbnail creation.
