#7358. Carl’s Jr. taps David&Goliath as marketing focus turns to boldness

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The agency of record appointment includes a mandate to lean into the QSR’s heritage and forward-looking initiatives like a Burger Revolution strategy.

Carl’s Jr. has appointed David&Goliath as marketing agency of record as it shifts focus to cooked-to-order burgers and tries to revive a bolder, boundary-pushing brand personality, according to news shared with Marketing Dive. Carl’s Jr. did not previously have a dedicated AOR, and instead worked with agencies on a project basis, Marketing Dive understands.

David&Goliath, which is part of Innocean Worldwide, will oversee brand strategy, creative development, experiential marketing, production and storytelling for the fast-food chain, with a mandate to lean into Carl’s Jr.'s heritage while shoring up cultural relevance with younger consumers. Its first work is expected to arrive in Q1 of next year.

CKE Restaurants Holdings-owned Carl’s Jr. unveiled its Burger Revolution strategy in September, which introduces a systemwide cooked-to-order approach to burger preparation. The announcement was accompanied by the release of a limited-time Angus Maximus 5.7-ounce burger. The changes are part of a larger effort by Carl’s Jr. to emphasize food quality, which has manifested in promotional areas like limited-time offerings.

Other fast-food companies, including rival Burger King, have thrown a spotlight on premium ingredients and restaurant improvements to win back price-sensitive diners. Carl’s Jr.’s franchised store count has declined in recent years. Franchisees of the brand and sister restaurant Hardee’s have faced their own profitability struggles, with a major one in Calirfornia in April declaring bankruptcy, Marketing Dive’s sister publication Restaurant Dive previously reported.

Carl’s Jr. has made internal changes to its marketing leadership this year as well. In the spring, CKE Restaurants named Burge Diemer, a restaurant industry vet who previously worked at brands including The Habit Burger & Grill, Boston Market and Jack in the Box, as CMO of Carl’s Jr. Diemer is tasked with developing breakthrough campaigns and driving product innovation. She credited David&Goliath with possessing the bravery necessary to build on Carl’s Jr.’s legacy.

“Together, we’re excited to push boundaries, expand our connection with customers, and bring the unmistakable Carl’s Jr. spirit to a new generation of burger lovers,” Diemer said in a press statement.

Carl’s Jr.’s advertising has not shied away from pushing buttons in the past. The chain in the 2000s became known for TV commercials featuring bikini-clad models suggestively eating burgers. It has dipped back into the racy well in recent years, including through a 2025 campaign with influencer Alix Earle that touted offerings like a hangover-themed burger.

#7356. Meta expands Muse to the UK

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The launch comes amid ongoing security concerns about what kind of user data the artificial intelligence agent may be accessing.

Meta has launched its Muse artificial intelligence agents in the U.K., which marks the next stage in the company’s expanded push to make Muse its key access point for consumer AI.

In order to launch its latest AI-powered tools in the U.K., Meta had to align with reporting and transparency regulations, as outlined by the U.K. Competition and Markets Authority. The CMA said that it had worked with Meta on its terms and conditions relating to Muse, in order to ensure that they align with existing consumer laws.

That could ensure greater protection for U.K. users, with the CMA also monitoring usage of the new app.

As per Meta: “From doing the Christmas shopping and searching for a cheaper energy deal, to sorting the school calendar or turning your saved travel Reels into a holiday itinerary, Muse can get it done for you. And from today, Meta’s personal AI agent, which proactively helps with your goals and suggests ideas, is available in the UK.”

Meta has partnered with a range of U.K. retailers and other businesses to maximize the utility of Muse right off the bat, including Marks & Spencer, Debenhams Group, Currys, Ocado Retail, Argos, Sainsbury’s, ASOS, JD Sports and more.

“With some [of these partners], you can connect your personal account so Muse can reorder your usual shop or pull up a booking,” Meta said. “With others, Muse can find its way around their websites from day one, so it can help you find what you need and get it done.”

As noted, Meta’s U.K. expansion is the latest in the company’s push to make Muse its next big platform, and realize its broader vision for consumer AI. The company launched Muse agents in Australia last week, while Muse is also available in the U.S., Canada, Japan and Singapore, with more regions set to come soon.

Though questions remain about the security of Muse, amid reports of unintentional misuse and vulnerabilities.

Shortly after Muse launched, a user in Toronto empowered his Muse agent to list and sell his items on Facebook Marketplace. The user then found that Muse had negotiated a deal, and organized for the buyer to pick up an item from his home address, without the user being aware of this process.

Further investigation found that the user had given Muse permission to do all of these tasks, though the user himself didn’t realize the level of authority that he had granted the app.

Which is at the core of a more recent security issue related to the AI bot.

According to a report from Reuters, Muse agents have been accessing users’ encrypted DMs in other apps, such as Signal, even when they don’t have explicit permission to do so. The Muse agents have been using systematic workarounds to avoid restrictions, and access more information than the user may have authorized.

As per Reuters: “Specifically, on Android, [Muse] used its permission to access the device's push notifications to retrieve the messages… On Apple’s macOS, it used a combination of the computer’s accessibility and screenshot tools, repurposing settings Apple offers to help people with disabilities operate their computers.”

So rather than directly accessing people’s private, encrypted DMs, which users may have restricted, and may feel are comfortably safe from the tool, Meta’s Muse agents can find other ways to track people’s private messages. This means that even without explicit access being granted to these tools, Meta’s AI bots can still gather private data.

Signal CEO Meredith Whittaker responded to these reports by further restricting Muse access to its platform.

As per Whittaker: “We also see a growing need for tools that can prevent third-party agents, like Meta’s Muse, from accessing application data using the deep permissions that users are encouraged to grant them during setup. In many cases these agents are leveraging accessibility settings that were meant to empower actual people to get the most out of their apps and services, not to act as a skeleton key that provides access to AI agents.”

The Signal incident highlights significant potential security vulnerabilities that could be exposed by Meta agentic tools, with Meta's AI systems able to problem-solve their way through access restrictions. The implications of that could be significant, especially if Muse can find workarounds to access banking information or health data that users may not actually want to share.

In response to these reports, Meta reiterated that users remain in control of the access that they grant Muse. But if those users don’t understand the technicalities of these processes, that assurance is largely meaningless.

In this context, it’s also worth noting that, according to data provided by Apptopia, around 46% of Muse users in the U.S. are over age 46.

According to data from the FBI, older users are more susceptible to online scams, and are seemingly less aware of the tools and processes that are in place to protect them. The FBI reported that in 2025, victims over 60 lost more than $7.7 billion to online scams, a 59% increase over 2024.

There's obviously some gap between the digital literacy of users aged under and over 50, but even so, the fact that older users are seemingly more willing to trust Muse could be setting the stage for further concerns.

According to data tracking conducted by First Page SEO, Muse is now up to 2.74 million daily active users, with shopping and research as its primary use cases.

#7355. Walmart is letting Meta’s Muse shop its shelves — but on its own terms

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

By letting Meta’s Muse agent into its stores only through the gateway it built and controls, Walmart is treating AI agent access the way retail media networks once treated ad slots: as inventory to be doled out on its own terms.

The retailer is preparing to launch a connector to Muse that will provide the AI agent with defined access to its e-commerce infrastructure, meaning it gets to set the guardrails and boundaries within which Meta’s agent can browse and shop.

The capability was noticed by Juozas Kaziukėnas, founder of e-commerce research firm Marketplace Pulse, after he spotted an update to Walmart’s technical instruction manual for Muse. According to The Verge, that integration launches tomorrow (Nov. 24), in time for Black Friday Cyber Monday shopping.

The manual, which Digiday has also seen and verified, describes how Muse can interact with Walmart’s shopping systems on behalf of a user. This includes tasks like searching for products, answering questions, building shopping carts and, if permission is granted, completing orders. Muse can also call on Walmart’s own shopping assistant Sparky to answer questions about products, stores and comparisons.

So a Walmart Shopper could ask Muse to compare three televisions, find specific ingredients for a dinner party, or ask the agent to add products to its Walmart shopping cart. Muse can then use Walmart’s systems to carry out those tasks. For example, Walmart could help Muse identify a customer’s usual brand of milk without handing over their entire shopping history.

This goes beyond what someone might typically expect from a chatbot, where a user might simply ask for recommendations. Instead, Muse, through the gateway to Walmart’s own marketplace, can act on those recommendations, taking care of the legwork involved in shopping and even making purchases once the user has given the necessary permission.

Walmart talked about its vision for this in its blog post last month.

Built using the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the integration gives AI agents a more direct and reliable way to interact with Walmart’s shopping systems. It’s designed to let agents shop on a customer’s behalf without giving them access to their wider purchase history or unnecessary personal information. For example, Walmart could help Muse identify a customer’s usual brand of milk without handing over their entire shopping history.

Walmart has also started introducing Agent Profiles, which gives each AI agent its own dedicated profile within a customer’s Walmart account. It means shoppers can distinguish purchases made by an AI agent from the ones they’ve completed themselves, while deciding how much autonomy they want to give the agent. Customers can require approval for every purchase, or set a spending limit (such as $50, $100 or $200), allowing the agent to spend up to that amount without seeking approval each time. Customers also have the ability to disable the agent’s access at any time.

This development comes after Amazon already blocked Muse from accessing its e-commerce site in September, arguing that third-party AI agents should operate openly and respect retailers’ decisions about whether to participate. At the time, Amazon said it asked Meta to remove its website from Muse’s shopping experience, but Meta declined. It also raised concerns about Muse accessing customer accounts without authorization and potentially capturing customer credentials. However, Meta disputed the claims, saying Muse cannot see users’ passwords or payment details.

While Walmart might be working closer with Muse going forward, this approach could raise questions about its ad business. In particular, with Muse increasingly allowed to take over product discovery, where does that leave its sponsored product placements and how much influence will brands have over what an AI agent recommends.

“There will emerge a new advertising mechanism where brands will pay dollars not for a sponsored placement, but for a ‘sponsored consideration’ to the agents,” said Abhishek Bora, head of digital growth at All Star Elite. “If agents take over the buying process, how would a new brand with a better product and offer get considered by an agent when it has no history of reviews, usage or purchases?”

Neither Walmart nor Meta responded to Digiday’s request for comment.

#7354. Intuit offloads Mailchimp to Bending Spoons to deepen bets on AI

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Bending Spoons, a technology conglomerate whose portfolio includes AOL and Eventbrite, will acquire the email automation company for $3.68 billion.

Intuit has entered into an agreement to sell email automation business Mailchimp to technology conglomerate Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion, the company confirmed in its latest earnings report. Intuit acquired Mailchimp in 2021 for $12 billion.

Intuit’s decision to sell comes as Mailchimp continues to be a drag on its business, which includes financial services QuickBooks, TurboTax and Credit Karma. The move is also positioned as a way to sharpen Intuit's focus on artificial intelligence and its other core products.

“We have built AI-native experiences to help businesses win new customers, manage their pipeline and help them grow through our lead-to-cash capabilities,” said Sasan Goodarzi, CEO of Intuit, on a call discussing the company’s latest earnings. “Selling Mailchimp sharpens our focus behind that strategy, while positioning Mailchimp and its team for continued success in their next chapter with Bending Spoons.”

Mailchimp, founded in 2001, was once the gem of the email marketing industry, but in the years following its acquisition by Intuit has struggled to maintain growth. Mailchimp’s revenue decreased 1% to $313 million during Q1 of the company’s fiscal 2027 for the period ended Oct. 31, a contrast to Intuit's overall revenue growth of 12% over the same period.

In May, Intuit announced that it was reducing its full-time workforce by 17% and “rightsizing” its investment in Mailchimp. As struggles persisted, the company in August revealed that it started running Mailchimp as a separate operating segment, a move that was intended to offer investors more transparency as Intuit tried to manage the unit for profitability.

The Mailchimp deal is expected to close in early 2027, at which point Bending Spoons plans to invest “substantially” in Mailchimp and build on its existing tools, according to a separate statement. Bending Spoons, an Italian company founded in 2013, acquires businesses and works to improve them with the goal of keeping them long-term. Other businesses acquired by the company include Vimeo, WeTransfer, Eventbrite, Streamyard and AOL.

Bending Spoons went public in July at a value of over $18 billion. Holding company Berkshire Hathaway commands a 4% ownership stake of the company.

Intuit last week launched a campaign — its first work with agency Mother New York — promoting the integration of its Intuit Intelligence agentic platform into QuickBooks. The campaign, “More Brains for your Business,” positions the AI capabilities as a helping hand instead of a replacement for human talent.

#7352. Why brands are writing no-AI clauses into creator deals

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

Influencer marketing contracts have become a focal point in the creator economy. There’s heightened attention being paid by brands, creators and creators’ representatives to deal terms, such as usage rights, exclusivity and payment terms. But among the newest addendums is AI usage.

“We actually are seeing more and more contracts including language around the creator not being able to use AI in their content for these campaigns,” said Kurt Stadelman, vp of talent at creator marketing firm Pearpop, in a conversation with Digiday managing editor Sara Jerde during Digiday’s recent Creator Strategies event.

Creators are actually welcoming brands’ no-AI demands, he said. Creators are already concerned about generative AI being used to create content and crowd out creators from people’s feeds. So brands forbidding AI-generated content from creators signals a commitment by brands to human-made content, said Stadelman.

But what counts as AI-generated content? Does it prohibit the creator from using AI tools in any part of their process?

“We’ve had to specify that a few times just to make sure, because obviously you want the creator to be able to use AI tools in the background when they’re developing their concept or their script. Even utilizing AI to analyze their past performance of their content and advise them on their strategy moving forward. And I think brands should probably embrace that because it ultimately helps the creator deliver the best version of themselves and the best content possible,” said Stadelman.

Here are a few highlights from the conversation, which have been edited for length and clarity.

It’s way too risky to be only utilizing organic posting for creator campaigns and just hoping that the right people see it. We are seeing more and more brands utilize paid behind whether it’s white-listing or utilizing the creator content as an ad unit for themselves on their own channels. Along with that comes, obviously, you have to write the paid usage rights into the contract, and most brands are good about that.

Usage in perpetuity should never be agreed to. That’s a dangerous place to be for a creator and can negatively impact their future collaborations with other brands in the same category. Exclusivity, obviously, is quite difficult for a lot of creators if they agree to a longer exclusivity term than they should. That limits their options moving forward.

Sometimes you’ll see proposed terms that are just a little too lengthy with the usage rights. We push back on that sometimes. I don’t think there’s any reason to be agreeing upfront to any more than six months of paid usage. Even that’s a bit lengthy. Starting it at three months if they’re really wanting to utilize paid with the campaign, that makes sense. Even up to six months is fine in most cases. But once you get to that point six months from now, you can reassess and extend if you’d like. But I don’t think there’s any reason to go beyond that in the initial contract.

We always push for shorter payment terms. If somebody’s asking for net-90, we try to push for net-60 or, ideally, net-30. But I understand that some brands have their standard operating procedures there, which is fine. But we just ask that they honor those payment terms, which is a whole other issue that we’re seeing happen more and more, is that brands are just not honoring these payment terms that they’ve themselves written into the contract.

#7351. Australian government moves ahead with algorithm opt-out legislation

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The proposed bill has passed another Senate hurdle, according to Australia’s ABC News.

The Australian government is moving to the next stage of implementing laws that would force social media platforms to provide algorithm opt-outs for all users.

In September, the Australian government announced that it would seek to implement legislation to enable all social media users to opt out of engagement-based algorithms. The move would let users switch to a chronological post order by default, ensuring that they would only see content from profiles that they have explicitly chosen to follow.

The landmark initiative could provide a valuable test case on the impacts of algorithms, and the data gleaned from that could form the basis for similar laws and restrictions in other markets.

Though various groups have opposed the concept, including U.S. authorities, which have raised concerns about localized censorship of content and control over U.S.-owned businesses.

However, the Australian government has now gained support to press ahead with the next stage of the plan.

As per reporting from Australia’s ABC News, the government reached a deal with the Australian Greens, a left-leaning political party, to secure support for the proposed bill, though the legislation did have to include some amendments.

As per ABC News: “Under Labor’s deal with the Greens, the maximum penalty for breaching the duty would be raised to up to 5 per cent of a platform's global revenue, rather than Labor's initial proposal of up to $109.2 million. The amendments also grant the government rule-making powers to establish a digital complaints ombudsman in the future to handle small claims and resolve minor issues.”

The proposal will also now include more specific examinations of potentially addictive design features.

Some political commentators and opponents of the legislation have raised concerns about the potential impact on free speech as a result of these laws.

Conservative commentator Michael Shellenberger recently suggested that the bill would give Australia’s eSafety Commissioner “sweeping powers over online speech, including the ability to operate fake social media accounts.”

The Australian government has amended the initial proposal to ensure that all content decisions are put to Parliament, and are not made by a single arbiter. Meanwhile, the government is also assessing a provision that allows researchers to create accounts to test whether platforms are adhering to the laws.

If approved, Australia's algorithm opt-out laws are projected to take effect from late 2027.

#7349. Chewy jumps on stop-motion animation trend lighting up holiday ads

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The brand’s research shows nearly 80% of pet owners plan to buy their furry friends at least one present this year.

In an effort to cut through generative artificial intelligence slop this holiday season, several brands have turned to what is considered to be one of the most labor-intensive forms of filmmaking: stop-motion animation. From Levi’s heartwarming claymation spot to Prada’s holiday effort which combines live actors with traditional 2D animation à la “Who Framed Roger Rabbit,” the technique has found itself the medium for many a holiday advertisement this year.

Pet supply company Chewy is no exception. Its holiday campaign marks the first time the brand has used the medium in a national TV spot. Stop-motion animation is used to portray the rich inner lives of pets during the holidays, where a Chewy box transports pets to a world of toys, treats and fun in the snow.

The idea was born out of the long-running Chewy Claus initiative, where owners can write to the company on behalf of their pets. As part of the effort, Chewy will help fund adoptions for shelter animals and send surprises to select letter-writers throughout the month of December.

“It didn't start with stop motion,” said Melissa Bell, Chewy’s chief brand officer, who joined the company in July. “We think about [the holidays] from our point of view, but given the importance of pets and animals for our company in particular, we were like,’ let's start with what our pets and animals think,’ and it naturally blossomed from there.”

Despite ongoing economic concerns potentially putting a damper on gift-giving this year, holiday pet spending continues to be a priority for many, especially for younger consumers. Nearly 80% of pet owners plan on buying a present for their animal this holiday season, with 21% of Gen Z and millennials planning to spend $100 or more, according to data from the brand. Chewy’s efforts go beyond the standard pet food and medication orders to encourage surprising the animals in one’s life and including them in the festive season.

The campaign marks the first time Chewy Claus is getting a national TV spot as part of the holiday campaign, according to Bell.

“The love and following of Chewy Claus is really inspirational, and for us, it was about connecting to…a bigger purpose because it's about helping shelter pets find homes. We wanted to bring that message to a larger audience, and this campaign gives us a way to bring that tradition to more people,” said Bell.

No AI was used in the creation of the spots, according to Bell. The puppets featured in the campaign were all crafted by hand and modeled after real-life animals. In the 30-second spot “A Holiday Dream,” a cat and dog are treated to a world of holiday whimsy created entirely in stop-motion animation. In the 15-second “A Holiday of Treats,” a dog is thrown a treat by a snowman dog toy, which he catches and crashes into a Chewy box filled with toys, before it ends with the dog asleep on the living room floor. Chewy’s in-house brands, such as Frisco, make frequent appearances.

Chewy’s holiday campaign expands beyond the national spot into a social media effort. Influencers, which the brand refers to as “Chewpanions” are central to the strategy and will be promoting the Chewy Claus effort, along with the brand more broadly.

In-person activations are also a key component of the effort and are largely centered around pet adoption. Chewy will host an event in Santa Monica, California, from Dec. 5-6, where attendees can write letters to Chewy Claus, explore a holiday market and meet adoptable pets. A similar event was held in Miami from Nov. 21-22 to kick off the season.

Chewy’s net sales totaled$3.33 billion, a 7.3% year-over-year increase, in its fiscal second quarter ending Aug. 2, per an earnings release. In February, Chewy acquired SmartPak, a horse supply and supplements brand. In May, it expanded its veterinary practice footprint through the acquisition of Modern Animal, bringing its approximate number of locations to 60.

#7347. Banking gets a helping hand in media modeling from SpendSight

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

It’s easy to know what your bank balance is, in the age of apps and online banking. It’s not as easy for banks to know how effective their marketing efforts are.

Mediastruction, an independent media agency that two years ago launched FutureSight, a SaaS platform dedicated to speeding up media mix modeling, is drilling into specific industries.

The brainchild of Marilois Snowman, who founded Mediastruction and FutureSight, SpendSight puts a specific lens onto the banking industry. It’s a free benchmarking tool that enables bank marketers to evaluate their media budgets to see if their spending aligns with their peers.

Snowman said conversations with clients and with other banks that aren’t yet clients told her there’s an information gap in the sector. “It’s a problem for mid market in general,” she explained in reference to other subscription media tools. “Sometimes mid-market brands don’t show up at all, or then they’re just wildly inaccurate.”

For small banks, this information is pretty important, agreed Mark Gibson, marketing practice leader at Capital Performance Group. “It’s not uncommon in the banking industry to have one or two people in the marketing department, and maybe not even an ad or media agency,” he said. “Media is like you know 1/20th of your job, so by definition, you’re not going to be very sophisticated about about what media is available and how you should allocate it. For that kind of advertiser, this kind of stuff can be really valuable.”

Snowman also noted that some media, from search to social and CTV, aren’t even properly tracked by other services. “Given the percentage of investment that is digital media these days — I mean, what isn’t digital media? — it just seems to be a big gap.”

Mediastruction built SpendSight from a proprietary 2026 survey of financial institution marketers, and Snowman said it’s the first of its kind to capture how banks and credit unions actually split paid media dollars across channels. To date, about 100 different banks and credit unions have participated in the survey, giving them access to the findings.

Any bank marketer enters their budget and channel mix, which lets SpendSight generate a side-by-side comparison against the peer average, flagging where they’re over- or under-invested. All inputs and responses to the survey remain anonymous and the underlying survey data is never exposed.

“All of that kind of discussion is really helpful for marketing teams to bring to executive leadership, and then to be able to sell through shifts in media plans and modeling engagements,” said Snowman.

So what has SpendSight determined? Initial results show some patterns with how banks and financial services have been marketing, and which media channels they’re relying on. Although it comes as no surprise that digital performance channels make up about 51% of the average media mix, broadcast and traditional media (linear TV, radio, print, out-of-home) still account for roughly 38%. (Interestingly, the American Bankers Association’s Banking Journal cited more than 60% digital spend, which Snowman attributed to differing channel definitions.)

Within digital, paid search and paid social represent more than one-fourth of average spend (13.7% and 13.0%, respectively). Paid search is the most widely used channel, with 96% of institutions investing in it. As for other media, direct mail makes up 7.4% of the average mix and is used by 82% of institutions, which is more than linear TV, display, and online video (as anyone knows who gets mail at home).

Gibson at Capital Performance Group, which participates in multiple surveys for banking including SpendSight, noted the reason he thinks SpendSight goes one step farther. “While [other studies] provide some useful benchmarking in terms of how much banks spend overall, and what various media are used, they don’t quantify the spend by media mix or by media channel,” he said. “That’s the new innovation that this tool does.”

It also gives Mediastruction lead generation to build up its potential client base with financial firms, which Snowman acknowledged. “What we really want to sell through is FutureSight’s modeling. We can use this as a free tool to get to know us to offer something of benefit to potential clients, that’s what our goal is.”

Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

We’re looking for a Software Engineer, AI Tooling Infrastructure to join our AI Tooling team and help build and run the backend services behind Supabase’s AI products. The Supabase MCP server is one example of what the team runs in production, alongside the services that support agent skills and the dashboard assistant. You’ll work closely with the Platform, SRE, Auth, Billing and Edge Functions teams, and with the engineers on the AI Tooling team who build the product surfaces.

The AI Tooling team runs its own services in production and carries its own on-call. Traffic from AI clients and agents behaves differently from traffic from people: hundreds of calls a minute, retry loops, and no reading of deprecation warnings. This role makes sure the services they use are reliable, correctly authorized and observable. It is a systems and infrastructure role rather than a product AI role, and it is not an SRE role. You will build and operate these systems, not only advise on them.

This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments, owns what they ship in production, and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions.

Build and operate the production backend services behind Supabase’s AI products, including the MCP server: deployment, scaling, configuration and release.

Take ownership of how those services are structured, including splitting or reshaping a service when that makes it safer to run and easier to change.

Define, measure and meet reliability targets for the services the team runs. Set SLOs with the SRE team, track error budgets, and use them to decide what to fix first.

Participate in the AI Tooling team on-call rotation, and be a first responder for incidents in those services. Investigate, fix, coordinate with other teams during incidents, and write the follow-ups and runbooks.

Work the AI Tooling team support queue alongside on-call, and turn recurring issues into fixes rather than repeated manual answers.

Own authentication and authorization for AI and agent clients: OAuth apps, scoped tokens, and permissions that make sense for agents as well as humans, including how we change or deprecate a permission without breaking existing integrations.

Own observability for the services the team runs: metrics, traces, logs, dashboards and alerts, so we find problems before customers do.

Handle capacity and abuse for agent traffic: rate limits, cost and safety controls, and behavior under load or when a dependency degrades.

Improve the architecture of the services the team owns as they grow, including splitting or reshaping a service when that makes it safer to run and easier to change.

Work with the Platform team on shared code, review ownership and release process, and with the SRE team on infrastructure, alerting and incident practice.

Contribute to the code of the AI Tooling team’s tools, such as the MCP server, where it affects reliability and security, in partnership with the engineers who own the product surface.

Have 5+ years of experience building and running backend services in production, and have carried on-call for them.

Write strong TypeScript or Go, and are comfortable working in the other.

Have designed and operated APIs with real consumers: versioning, error handling, rate limiting, and backwards-compatible change.

Know OAuth, OIDC, JWT and API authorization well enough to debug them in production and to explain where implementations commonly deviate from the spec.

Have a good understanding of PostgreSQL and relational databases.

Are comfortable with CI/CD, Docker and containerized deployments, and with infrastructure as code. Any tool is fine.

Can debug across services: follow a slow or failing request through several systems using metrics, traces and logs.

Communicate clearly in writing, work with a wide range of stakeholders, and thrive in async, globally distributed teams.

Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and moving quickly.

Pick your centre of gravity. We expect you to be deep in at least one of these, and to tell us which:

APIs and auth: You have designed permission models, token scopes or OAuth flows for third-party or machine clients, and you have migrated them without breaking users.

Gateways and distributed systems: You have built or run proxies or gateways, or debugged hard failures across services (retries, partial failures, upstream outages, fail-open vs fail-closed decisions), and you can reason about load and degradation.

Experience with agent tooling (MCP or similar), or serving traffic from AI agents and LLM clients.

Experience moving a service out of a larger codebase while keeping existing clients working.

Experience with Grafana, OpenTelemetry, Logflare or a similar observability stack, and real SLO work.

Open-source contributions, especially to Node.js, Go, TypeScript or API tooling.

#7343. In Graphic Detail: How shoppers are adopting AI for product research ahead of Black Friday

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

Marketers are shifting ad dollars toward performance channels as the important Black Friday/Cyber Monday trading period approaches. Yet the way consumers use search — a crucial channel within performance marketing — is evolving rapidly, as they adopt generative AI tools like Gemini and ChatGPT to aid their purchasing decisions.

The places they find information about brands, the sources that information is based on, and what they do with that information are all changing. Meanwhile, audience adoption of AI research is far from uniform across generations and markets, further complicating the picture.

“Black Friday used to be won in the final week with the deepest discount and the loudest media,” said Jonathan Verrall, vp of SEO at Jellyfish. “Now AI writes the shortlist weeks earlier from the sources shoppers trust. Advertisers who treat Black Friday as pure promo media are already late. The winners will plan earned, owned and paid together from October and give AI data it can believe.”

What is certain is that the way brands seek to influence consumers during product discovery and research is shifting. With the year’s biggest sales event around the corner, read on for a data snapshot of the state of product discovery.

According to a survey of 2,800 shoppers in the U.S. and U.K. conducted by Brainlabs in 2025 and 2026, the percentage of consumers using AI for product research rose on average from 6% last year to 13%. Clearly, more shoppers are using AI tools to compare and research the products they’re considering. While search engines themselves still led consumer practices, sources like Amazon and YouTube slipped.

A Jellyfish study of citation sources, using U.K. Black Friday-related prompts the week beginning Nov. 16, found third-party sources leading the pack. That means blogs, news articles and comparison sites counted for more than brands’ own websites or retail listings in influencing AI chatbot representations of a brand or a product.

This is borne out by other studies. In an analysis run for an unnamed client, PMG found a brand’s website supplied just 24 out of 203 links cited in AI answers recommending the client’s products. Only 22 went directly to its homepage.

Even if they only account for a minority of citations, brands’ own sites, platforms and retailer listings are areas that an advertiser can control. Zooming in, not all retail platforms are equal, either. Amazon, Costco and Etsy’s sites have lost share of citations in recent quarters, while Target and Walmart have gained in recent months, according to data from Tinuiti and Profound.

The hope that they might influence shoppers using AI tools for product discovery has been one of the motivations driving marketing dollars toward ChatGPT. Ad spend has risen month-on-month, according to estimates by AdClarity, which estimated total spend on the platform to have reached $116.6 million in October, with U.S. brands accounting for 64%. (The above chart is in millions of dollars.)

Issues with measurability and evidence that ChatGPT ads lead to greater conversions, however, may hold brands back from accelerating that spend as much as OpenAI execs would like.

According to Bain, two-thirds of consumers use AI tools for general research, while 42% specifically use them to research products. But there are variations across generations.

The McKinsey Agentic Commerce Consumer Survey, June 2026, surveyed 5,800 shoppers who’s used AI chatbots or search tools for a shopping task in the last three months. It found middle-aged and younger consumers are embracing the tech while older shoppers (who still hold plenty of disposable income) aren’t. It’s an important distinction for brands targeting consumers in specific stages of their lives.

As social trends accelerate, brands like General Mills are scoring creator posts for shareability to bridge the gap between organic buzz and paid media.

Dick’s is betting that youth sports can fuel its next phase of ad growth through GameChanger—if it can overcome limits on scale.

As Black Friday Cyber Monday rapidly approaches, brands are most focused on acquiring new customers this holiday season.

#7340. The clipping economy is changing as platforms crack down and creators seek control

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

Depending on who you ask in the creator economy, they might say that clipping is dead.

The practice of sharing short clips from long-form content to boost the original content’s audience or promote a brand, exploded in popularity over the last few years, with major creators like Jimmy “MrBeast” Donaldson, Cody “Clix” Conrod, and Eric “Airrack” Decker starting their own clipping companies. It catapulted certain creators into the spotlight and encouraged brands to hire clippers to give their branded partnerships extra airtime.

In short, what began as fans sharing clips has grown into a billion-dollar distribution business.

But some platforms are now tightening the rules around clipping. TikTok and YouTube have been cracking down on non-original and mass reposting content. Last week, Instagram added a content protection feature previously available only on Facebook, which lets eligible creators automatically identify videos matching their original content. They can now see how those videos perform and decide whether to hide them from people on the platform, add a credit link, or let the videos stay up. That gives creators more visibility and control over where their content appears, making clipping less of an open-ended reporting play and more subject to the original creator’s say.

“Creators deserve credit for the work they make,” a Meta spokesperson told Digiday. “[This] builds on our broader efforts to prioritize and reward original content and creativity over re-uploaded posts that don’t add a unique perspective or meaningful edits.”

And yet, platforms aren’t all moving in the same direction: Twitch is investing further into clipping to try and claw back the short-form real estate it’s ceded to other platforms. To understand what’s driving these diverging approaches, and what they mean in practice, Digiday spoke with seven experts across the clipping ecosystem.

“Ask 10 people [what clipping is] and you’ll probably get eight different answers,” said Darren Clover, CEO of creator-led holding company Full Box Inc., which owns Reach Clipping. “We define clipping as skilled editors taking existing source material and transforming it into unique pieces of short-form content…Those videos are then distributed across individual social accounts. That’s very different from downloading someone else’s TikTok and reposting the exact same video across hundreds of accounts.”

Opinions also differ around whether clipping works as a performance marketing channel or if it’s just a good distribution method. A few days ago, Brian Blum, host of the Only Sweat Equity podcast, posted on X that clipping “has actually always been dead.” He told Digiday he meant that it has never worked as a performance marketing channel.

Blum’s concern is that clipping can produce impressive view counts without reaching people likely to buy. He said campaigns can be vulnerable to fraud and attract audiences that may not be a fit for the product.

“It doesn’t have necessary protections to prevent viewbotting or fraud…So you’re actually just lighting money on fire,” he said.

Nikolai Amirzadeh, co-founded of clipping company Clip Tech, said clips can function as both marketing and distribution tools if the clipping company in question does the work to ensure views are valid.

“It is priced like performance, you pay per 1,000 verified views and nothing for clips that flop. It behaves like earned media, because it is native posts from real accounts, not ads. Brands typically pay $1 to $4 per thousand verified views, against $10 to $80 or more for traditional paid social,” Amirzadeh said. “Anything that looks off goes to the fraud team, and the clipper is not paid until it is cleared. A view is still a view by each platform’s own definition, which is a low bar. That is why the serious brands look at the top clips, watch time and what happens downstream, not just the view total.”

Then there’s the question of control: As clipping spreads and platforms tighten their rules, creators and their partners are increasingly concerned about how clips are edited and shared, and whether they could create brand-safety risks.

“Clipping is kind of a double-edged sword. It can help creators gain visibility and show that people value their content, but it could also get them flagged as spam,” said Ashray Urs, head of Streamlabs.

That lack of control gives creators and their managers pause, according to Reed Duchscher, CEO of Night Management. “It’s hard to control any of it,” he said. “Even when you put out a bounty for someone to clip something, you still have very limited control of what is posted, how it’s posted,” he added, pointing to the common practice of people clipping streamers out of context to farm outrage or drama.

Instead, their clients, like mega creator Kai Cenat, have their own in-house clippers, which allows for more control and, crucially, legitimate measurement.

Expect this to be an increasingly popular approach in the next year. “Sometimes with these clipping companies you can’t understand if the views are legitimate or not…you don’t know if they’re paid views or not paid views because you’re not controlling the TikTok accounts and not posting the videos. So we’re a little nervous about that,” Duchscher said.

With platforms cracking down on recycled content, the age of the clip farm may be over. But clipping itself isn’t.

Mustafa Aijaz, vp of media company SoaR, thinks clipping is no longer a low-effort gold rush. “A quick cut and post won’t get you very far,” he said. “You need a different caption, some commentary, or a breakdown — something that adds to the raw clip itself. If you’re different, the platform treats you differently. But if you look exactly like the other posts, you’ll likely be throttled.”

And as the demand for clips has grown, some have leaned into the more negative aspects of clipping, like taking creators out of context or clipping moments that are less than flattering. This influx of negative framing or drama farming has shifted creators’ opinions on external clippers.

Add that to the clipping companies’ increased selectiveness and rising rates, and something’s gotta give, according to Brandy Merriweather, founder and senior PR executive at BSTarPR.

“Many successful clipping pages have secured partnerships with gambling entities, music labels, creator management companies, creator collectives, and streaming platforms. Consequently, they are becoming more selective about which creators they post, their rates, and the frequency of posting for specific creators,” she said.

Merriweather told Digiday she’s seen creators have to pay extra money to clippers to switch priority streaming platforms.

“It’s a BIG business filled with egos, narrative control, fabricated numbers, unethical and sometimes purposely false content all going to the highest bidder,” she said. To avoid price gouging or unfair depictions, creators need to take clipping into their own hands. “What used to be a vehicle to gain visibility has now turned into an accountability stage that creators have no control over since many don’t own these pages. The creators, their families, and their teams are being used to create drama and fuel negativity which algorithms have prioritized because of the engagement….It’s a system many helped build that now controls them.”

Merriweather’s solution matches the other experts Digiday spoke with: creators have to create their own clipping networks to ensure they have control over their content and a proper understanding of how it’s performing.

#7339. How Hershey strategized its brand film to be more than a 90-minute ad

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Filmmakers worked with the company, gaining access to archives and historians and collaborating on IP, brand and creative considerations.

“Hershey,” a biopic of Hershey Company founder Milton S. Hershey, hits theaters on Wednesday. The film, along with the marketer’s celebration of America’s 250th anniversary, are expected to contribute almost one percentage point to company sales in 2026, CEO Kirk Tanner said on a recent earnings call. “Hershey” has so far earned strong customer and retail response.

“It's relevant for our time, so we’ve seen a lot of support and that's going to show up in-store with inventory in displays and a connection back to the movie ... That will be an uplift. That will be a tailwind for the portfolio and especially Hershey, which has already had a terrific year,” Tanner said. “We like the momentum that will build going into 2027.”

What sets “Hershey” apart from other branded films is the way that the filmmakers worked with the company, gaining access to Hershey archives and historians and collaborating on intellectual property, brand and creative considerations.

“We wanted a real story told, which means, as a marketer, you need to gulp a little bit and say, ‘Hey, it's not a story if there's no conflict.’ You only get a tiny bit of that [conflict] when you create advertisements,” said Suzanne Jones, vice president of the Hershey Experience at The Hershey Company. “We wanted to make sure this was not in any way, shape or form a 90-minute commercial.”

"Hershey” is the product of a collaboration between the Hershey entities — the combination of The Hershey Company, Milton Hershey School, Hershey Entertainment & Resorts, The M.S. Hershey Foundation and Hershey Trust Company — with production company Dandelion Media. The film was produced in association with Aloe Entertainment, Peachtree Group and RCM3 with UTA Independent Film Group.

“This is not just a story about something that happened in the past, but it is a living legacy that exists today, and not just in the candy bar, but in the Milton Hershey School,” Jones said. “There are kids across town sitting in algebra class because of what Milton and Catherine Hershey did. It's way more than the story of a founder or the story of a brand.”

The content of the “Hershey” film sets it apart from a rash of recent branded films from E.l.f., Garage Beer and Texas Pete that mostly used humor to market products and value propositions. The film focuses on the story of Milton Hershey, whose grit and perseverance led not only to a $35 billion snack company, but also a series of charitable organizations.

“Consumers today are really looking for authenticity and what a brand stands for in the products that it delivers to the marketplace, but its role in the community and in society today, as well,” Jones said.

For Hershey, the film is at the heart of an ecosystem that spans channels and its portfolio, which includes Reese's, Twizzlers and salty snacks like Dot's Pretzels. The brand on Wednesday will sell Hershey bars via Amazon and Walmart at their original 5-cent price, and will release limited-edition, vintage-inspired packaging featuring QR codes that link to more information about the Hershey story.

“As we've looked at activating against this, we've been able to … collaborate with our retail partners across the country to bring the film to life,” Jones said. “It wasn't this insurmountable lift to marry the Hershey's brand to the equity of the film because it is so authentically intertwined.”

Beyond retail, Hershey will utilize social and creator content, as well as some surprises for consumers during the holiday week. The company has been working to develop its muscle around social media, including through posts tied to cultural moments like the recent Microsoft shutdown and the release of “Grand Theft Auto VI.”

Hershey kicked off the year with its first major creative effort in eight years, launching the “It’s Your Happy Place” platform ahead of the 2026 Olympic and Paralympic Winter Games. The brand subsequently partnered with girl group Katseye on a fully integrated campaign around its new Creme Bars. The Hershey Company reported net sales growth of 3% in Q3, with North American confectionery business sales growth of 1.6%.

#7337. Digiday+ Research: A-Frame Brands, Ritual and other brands prioritize new customer acquisition this holiday season

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

This research is based on unique data collected from our proprietary audience of publisher, agency, brand and tech insiders. It’s available to Digiday+ members. More from the series →

As Black Friday and Cyber Monday rapidly approaches, brands are most focused on acquiring new customers this holiday season. They’re also eager to turn those seasonal shoppers into repeat buyers.

Fifty-nine percent of brand and retailer professionals said that new customers are the primary audience for their 2026 holiday advertising. That’s down just one percentage point from the 60% of marketers who said the same last year, indicating that customer targeting trends have not shifted significantly.

Less than half of survey respondents (41%) said that existing customers are the main audience for their holiday marketing, up one percentage point from 40% in 2025.

The holiday season’s influx of shoppers gives brands an annual opportunity to attract new customers and to build lasting relationships beyond the initial purchase.

Ari Bloom, founder and CEO of brand incubator A-Frame Brands, estimates that brands see a 20% to 30% increase in new customers as a percentage of total during the holiday season, as consumers look to discover products and brands. “It is a time period where you can acquire a lot of new customers… when we naturally see new customers come into the holiday funnel,” Bloom said.

He also expects AI to play a central role in 2026 holiday marketing, changing how consumers find and buy products. “AI is probably going to become one of the most important funnels for new customers because, instead of using old habits to discover existing brands, there’s a whole other ‘person’ shopping for them,” Bloom said. “Just as we see people relying more on AI agents, you’re going to see more new brand exploration and customer acquisition from the brand side.”But acquiring new customers is only part of the equation. Brands also need to give existing customers a reason to return.

Laura Brodie, chief growth officer at supplement company Ritual, said brands can encourage repeat purchases by offering exclusive perks, seasonal products and other incentives. “Being able to pull people back who have shopped before by creating a compelling gift with purchase, seasonal drop or something similar is one way,” Brodie said. “If you don’t have the budget to support units, having something that feels intentional for an existing customer base is another.”

Brands with similar consumer bases should also consider partnering on gift-with-purchase offers, according to Brodie. “The cost of acquisition is high during the holidays, so being able to tap an existing audience can be really cost-effective,” she said. “Similar-sized brands can create something that feels compelling [to consumers] and benefits both brands — potentially an offer swap. We’ve had success partnering with brands like Osea on a swap gift with purchases.”

As social trends accelerate, brands like General Mills are scoring creator posts for shareability to bridge the gap between organic buzz and paid media.

Dick’s is betting that youth sports can fuel its next phase of ad growth through GameChanger—if it can overcome limits on scale.

#7332. Geico unites brand icons in holiday ad mixing human craft, nostalgia

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

A stop-motion narrative video complements the insurance firm’s first appearance with a float at the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.

Geico is making a more concentrated push around the holidays with a festive holiday ad and Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade float. The insurance firm is celebrating its 90th anniversary this year, and both the float and the narrative-driven video bring together a cast of characters drawn from a legacy of memorable TV commercials. The Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade itself is promoting its centennial, which has attracted additional brand interest this year.

“How 15% Saved Christmas” aligns with a larger trend of marketers focusing on content that seeks to stoke a sense of nostalgia in viewers. The effort uses stop-motion animation recalling Rankin/Bass holiday classics while leaning into fondness for mascots such as the Gecko and Caveman. Following the Thanksgiving Day Parade, the ad will air in theaters across 12 markets through Dec. 27. Geico plans to run additional holiday creative, including a seasonal spin on its “Hump Day” ad, during streaming and football programming.

Geico’s team of animators sketched the setting and core characters for “How 15% Saved Christmas” and the puppets were made by hand. AI was used in the pre-visualization phase while the background environments were produced with a hybrid approach combining AI generated-imagery with practical sets to create the appearance of a matte painting.

The renewed emphasis on human craft among marketers has been interpreted as a response to growing AI backlash. A number of other brands, including Chewy, Prada and Levi’s, are also leveraging old-school animation techniques for their holiday campaigns this year. Coca-Cola, which ran AI-generated campaigns the past two years, is pivoting back to ads featuring real humans.

This is the first time the Geico characters have appeared together in a holiday campaign, which tells the story of a town that has seen its Christmas spirit hit an all-time low. Santa is able to reach Maxwell the Pig over a ham radio — as in, a radio shaped like a literal leg of ham — with a message around saving Christmas and 15%, a key part of Geico’s messaging. There are also 15 hidden Easter eggs in “How 15% Saved Christmas” that nod to past Geico work.

Martin, the brand’s longtime agency, developed the campaign, which was created in partnership with production company Passion Pictures Animation, stop-motion specialist studio Screen Novelties and Mackinnon & Saunders. The float was unveiled in September and has been promoted through a 10-week, cross-country tour in the lead up to Thanksgiving.

"Geico has always been an entertainment brand, and people still quote our characters years after they were first introduced," said Geico CMO Arianna Orpello in a press statement. "This season, we wanted to give people something they could simply enjoy.”

Orpello became CMO of Geico in January, joining the insurance marketer from Goldman Sachs.

#7331. Dick’s Sporting Goods is turning youth sports into a premium ad business

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

Dick’s Sporting Goods has found that there’s big business in youth sports.

The sporting retailer recorded a third quarter GAAP net income of $161 million in earnings this week — more than double the $75 million reported the year prior.

Dick’s execs attributed much of that success to Dick’s Media Network, home to its youth sports app GameChange.

Like many long-tail retail media networks, Dick’s Sporting Goods doesn’t break out its ad business revenue by dollar figure or percentage. Dick’s chief financial officer Navdeep Gupta noted that the company is grappling with supply-chain related costs, higher fuel costs and other pressures, but Dick’s Media Network partially offset those pressures.

“We have talked about these gross margin growth drivers with Dick’s Media Network and GameChanger. Those are continuing to be very differentiated drivers of not only our profitability, but our gross margin expansion,” he said.

Dick’s Media Network is four years old and offers ad units in-store, on its own site, off-site across the open web, social and streaming. Perhaps its biggest get is its live sports via GameChanger.

“They found this gap in the marketplace in terms of sports club video streaming. And they’ve created this app, this solution, and now they inherently have their own O&O [owned and operated] inventory from a media perspective,” said Olivia Hawkins, vp of media strategy at Salt XC.

Dick’s has previously worked with sports brands like Adidas, On, Under Armor and Crocs. However, the sports retailer is actively engaging non-endemic partners too.

Take Chobani, for example. The yogurt brand bought ad space on Dick’s Sporting Goods Game Changer app during the 2026 FIFA World Cup, said Hawkins, who was familiar with the deal.

She did not disclose financial details of the ad buy. The campaign focused on reach and awareness, getting Chobani in front of youth sports enthusiasts, like parents and coaches, Hawkins said.

“They met our expectations in terms of reaching a new audience and delivery, frequency, and all those media metrics — CPM and video completions and all that,” she said, without detailing the campaign’s success.

Dick’s video app CPMs are more premium, hovering around $35, according to one commerce executive who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

“That’s more expensive than big TV. They’re asking for that price for that type of inventory. It’s a great solution — super clever, but it’s expensive,” the anonymous exec told Digiday. In comparison, Netflix CPMs fell from their initial $60 when it launched in 2022 to the low $20s currently.

Seemingly, brands are willing to cough up the dough. That’s the bet Dick’s seems to be making. It makes sense given sports has become the industry’s latest golden goose.

Put some numbers on it. In a survey this year, Dick’s Media and eMarketer reported that 63% of U.S. parents have kids in youth sports and 84% of them said youth sports influence their buying choices.

Now, there’s the question of scale. Dick’s GameChanger app has more than 5 million monthly active users, but youth sports is more niche than something like the National Football League, which averages 18.7 million viewers per game during the regular season.

“It’s a great audience. It’s a great inventory, but it is finite versus other offsite environments that include all of the open web,” Hawkins said.

That leaves Dick’s in the same boat as other retail media networks — or at least every other RMN that isn’t Amazon or Walmart — where continued growth may have to come from beyond retailers’ owned and operated channels.

#7327. Brands race to systematize how to know what makes creator content worth paying for

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

Social media trends move faster than brands can keep up with. Now, they’re trying to create repeatable systems to turn organic social attention into something they can evaluate, fund and ultimately scale.

Take General Mills, for example. Home to brands like Cheerios, Cinnamon Toast Crunch and Trix, the CPG brand has spent the past year putting together an internal framework to systematize monetizing viral moments.

Its “talkability score” is a calculation used to measure whether General Mills’ brands are earning more attention with social media creators than they’re buying with paid ads. It’s a loose framework that varies by brand, Mindy Murray, director of influencer and content at General Mills said, and generates a score based on whether users shared it, put their own spin on it and how long interest in the trend lasts.

Murray was mum on the actual mechanics on how it actually determines whether to invest ad spend. “We’re weighing on earning, we’re weighing things like active engagement — so shares likes, comments, saves — because we know that that means someone took an actual effort to do something versus just an impression,” Murray said.

Virality can’t be manufactured, but this “operating system” allows them to “go faster and be smarter,” said Murray.

Over the past year, General Mills has also reorganized its teams to bring social and influencer marketing under Murray’s purview, she told Digiday, to move more quickly and efficiently in converting buzzy organic content into paid ads.

For example, over the summer Reese’s “Eat ‘Em Up” cereal jingle from the early 2000s started trending on TikTok. General Mills noticed the trend, partnered with GloRilla to re-record the rap, tracked real-time activity via its framework, and ultimately turned it into a campaign on streaming platforms and Reese’s Puffs’ YouTube channel. The company boasted a 2.5% year-over-year sales increase as a result, but did not provide specific sales figures. The company did not say specifically how the framework informed that strategy.

Last week, influencer agency Billion Dollar Boy (BDB) rolled out its Creator Investment Planner, a financial modeling tool that aims to help marketers understand the ad spend levels required to plan and “de-risk creator investments,” according to a news release.

BDB’s tool works by calculating blended CPMs from creators and social media platforms. Marketers enter their budget and time frame, and the platform calculates estimates for share of voice, total impressions and earned media value. Per BDB, the model can update as inputs change, where marketers can expect to “de-risk” spend commitments.

And in April, CreatorIQ creator platform and creative analytics and governance platform CreativeX launched a new tool to help brands incorporate creator content into a paid media strategy. The system works on an API, sending creator content from CreatorIQ’s platform to CreativeX to be graded, reviewed by CreativeX’s AI-powered system and optimized by a brand campaign manager. Ultimately, it aims to identify creator posts with potential to do well as an ad before any media buyers open their wallets. Nestlé was the first brand to sign on. The integration was announced on an invite-only basis.

To agency execs, all signs point to brands getting more rigorous about their spend — especially when it comes to squeezing performance out of creators — and do it before the trend disappears.

Creator spend is expected to increase 12% every year until 2030, according to advertising research firm Madison & Wall. In no small part, brand spend on boosting or promoting creator content is fueling that growth.

“Before any sort of budget is unlocked, you have to be able to prove out that there’s a higher propensity for that piece of content for whatever investment you’re making into social to actually move towards a conversion,” said Madison Gaudry-Routledge, evp of social at Viral Nation, a social agency.

Most brands, Gaudry-Routledge said, haven’t come up with a named framework in the same way General Mills has. Brand spend on creator marketing is expected to grow twice as fast as spending on advertising. Naturally, brands are eager to see proof of concept as early as possible.

Viral Nation has its own proprietary framework offered to clients as an add-on service. It’s called Culture Quotient that blends brand awareness, brand affinity and brand velocity into a measurable score to determine a brand’s relevance in cultural conversation. The tool works via AI that analyzes conversations and content, identifies emerging cultural trends and tracks shifts in consumer sentiment, per Gaudry-Routledge. The social exec declined to share any client-specific examples.

These calculations are being built in real time and haven’t yet replaced traditional metrics like share of voice, audience sentiment and engagement.

“As an industry, we’re continuing to try to catch up on operationalizing frameworks and systematizing measurement and still not there yet,” said Kristina Coughlin, svp and general manager of Trevant, a creator marketing agency.

Dick’s is betting that youth sports can fuel its next phase of ad growth through GameChanger—if it can overcome limits on scale.

As Black Friday Cyber Monday rapidly approaches, brands are most focused on acquiring new customers this holiday season.

Product discovery habits are changing, leaving marketers unsure how to pivot ahead of the biggest sales period of the year.

We're backed by a16z, Sequoia, and Redpoint, and proud to operate as a globally distributed team that values high agency, direct communication, and customer love.If you want to build the infrastructure that lets every engineering team - and every agent they deploy - operate on their codebase with confidence, join us.

#7311. Growth Copywriter at Winona

Winona is one of the leading telemedicine companies providing HRT for women in menopause. We’ve built all of our technology in house including an EHR, patient care admin system, patient portal, website, marketing technology etc. Winona has two compounding pharmacies and a team of in house physicians providing world-class care via a fully vertically integrated business model.

We are looking for a data-backed, empathetic Growth Copywriter to own the performance and optimization of our end-to-end messaging ecosystem. At Winona, copy isn’t just about sounding nice. It’s a measurable variable in our growth funnel. You will design and execute rapid copy experiments across our paid acquisition, intake flows, and lifecycle retention loops to help women confidently access bioidentical HRT and menopause care.

Full-Funnel Experimentation. Write copy hypotheses, design rapid A/B tests alongside growth and analytics teams, analyze performance data, and turn winning variations into a scalable messaging playbook.

Lifecycle Growth & Retention. Write, test, and optimize automated onboarding, activation, adherence, churn-save, and win-back sequences across email, SMS, and push notifications to drive LTV.

High-Intent Conversion Surfaces. Own the persuasive strategy and microcopy for landing pages, interactive quiz/intake flows, checkouts, and dynamic pricing/offer messaging.

Paid Acquisition at Scale. Generate volume-driven concepts, hooks, and static/video copy variants for Meta, Google, and YouTube, systematically iterating based on creative testing data.

Voice of Customer (VoC) Intelligence. Continuously mine product reviews, customer support tickets, intake data, and exit surveys to isolate deep qualitative insights and high-converting customer language.

AI-Augmented Workflows. Leverage and train Winona’s internal AI copywriting tools to scale production velocity, maintain brand consistency, and build automated variant pipelines without sacrificing quality.

5+ years of dedicated copywriting experience specializing in direct-response, conversion copywriting, or growth marketing.

DTC Telehealth, Wellness, or HealthTech experience is highly preferred. You understand how to write about sensitive health topics with clinical authority and deep empathy.

A portfolio backed by data and results — the exact copy variants you tested, the structural or psychological changes you made, and the quantifiable lift they produced in metrics like CTR, quiz completion, or conversion rates.

Deep lifecycle marketing mastery: significant experience building and optimizing automated email and SMS flows (onboarding, retention, win-backs), rather than just writing one-off promotional campaigns. You know how to nurture a lead over time.

A strong foundation in A/B testing mechanics — comfortable formulating clear copy hypotheses, understanding sample size requirements, and knowing when a test result has achieved true statistical significance.

The balance of empathy and compliance: a proven ability to write about highly sensitive personal health topics (menopause symptoms, hormonal changes, wellness) with profound empathy while strictly adhering to healthcare compliance rules and ad-network medical restrictions.

An experimenter’s ego — you don’t take copy critiques personally. You’re obsessed with letting consumer behavior and performance data crown the winning angle.

As a full-time member of our team, you’ll enjoy:

Paid non-working holidays per country of residence

Medical/ Dental/ Vision insurance (US-W2)

Employee engagement activities and virtual gatherings

#7309. Target’s New AI Assistant Is Just For Browsing, For Now

Ask Target is now available to all shoppers after initially testing the feature with Target employees.

#7306. Cadence Health: Registered Nurse - Float Pool

Headquarters: Remote

Cadence is the clinical AI company automating the treatment of chronic disease. Its Clinical Intelligence takes on the routine, high-volume work of chronic care – monitoring patients, surfacing risks, and coordinating action – so clinicians can focus on the decisions that require them. Grounded in partnerships with more than 20 leading health systems, deep EMR integrations, dedicated medical group, and experience serving a population of more than 100,000 patients, the system learns from real-world care delivery, improving as it scales. Cadence has been recognized by TIME as one of the Top 100 HealthTech Companies and by LinkedIn as a Top Startup (#4, 2025).

The Float Pool Registered Nurse supports Cadence patients by monitoring the alert board, responding to urgent clinical needs, and providing flexible coverage across care delivery workflows. This role requires a highly adaptable RN who can move seamlessly between alert monitoring, triage, and care management support to ensure continuity of care for patients with chronic conditions.

Licensure Requirements

  • Active Compact Multi-State RN license
  • Active RN licensure in one or more of the following states: CA, NY, or HI

Schedule Requirements:

  • Option 1: Alternating 3x12 / 4x12 Schedule
    • 12-hour shifts from 8:00 AM to 8:00 PM in your local time zone
    • Schedule: Thursday, Friday, Saturday, with every other Wednesday

    Option 2: Fixed 4x10 Schedule
    • 10-hour shifts from 8:00 AM to 7:00 PM in your local time zone
    • Schedule : Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday

Note: All schedules include a one-hour unpaid lunch break.

What You’ll Do

  • Monitor patient vitals, symptoms, and lab data via the alert board to identify patients in need of clinical intervention
  • Respond to inbound patient clinical questions and escalations by phone and text message
  • Conduct timely outreach to patients with abnormal readings to assess clinical status and triage appropriately
  • Follow established triage protocols to determine next steps, including provider escalation, after-hours care, emergency referral, or 911 activation when necessary
  • Document all patient interactions, assessments, and interventions accurately in the Cadence platform
  • Support virtual follow-ups with patients to reinforce care plans, medication adherence, and lifestyle goals
  • Assist with care coordination and development of clinical summaries for patients’ physicians
  • Provide flexible coverage across clinical programs, including alert monitoring, CCM, and APCM, based on daily staffing needs
  • Help Cadence scale exceptional care delivery for patients with CHF, hypertension, diabetes, and other chronic conditions
  • Contribute to continuous improvement of workflows and clinical processes
  • Be instrumental in delivering an exceptional patient experience aligned with Cadence’s care standards and health system goals

What you need

  • Active RN compact multi-state license.
  • Associate Degree in Nursing.
  • 5+ years of clinical nursing experience in outpatient, inpatient, chronic care, telehealth, or related settings.
  • Strong experience with clinical triage, including telephone or virtual triage.
  • Critical care or emergency nursing experience strongly preferred.
  • Experience supporting Chronic Care Management programs preferred.
  • Strong clinical judgment and ability to work independently.
  • Ability to monitor patient vitals, symptoms, and labs to identify care needs.
  • Ability to follow up with patients to gather clinical information and triage appropriately.
  • Excellent verbal, written, and interpersonal communication skills.
  • Comfort working across multiple systems and technologies.
  • Passion for delivering high-quality, patient-centered care.
  • Adaptability and flexibility in a fast-paced, remote environment.

The anticipated base salary range for this role is $85,000 to $95,000 annual base salary, which is based on role scope, level, and location. In addition to base compensation, this role may be eligible for incentive compensation as part of the overall total rewards package. This position is remote and based in the United States. Actual compensation will be determined based on factors including experience, skills, internal equity, and applicable law.

Benefits & Perks

  • Competitive pay & equity*
  • Fully remote
  • Comprehensive health coverage: Medical, dental & vision
  • Paid time off
  • 401k plan + matching
  • Paid parental leave
  • Home office stipend

*benefit offerings may vary depending on job profile, job level and worker type
